_**Victory Salute**_, commonly referred to as the **Olympic Black Power Statue**, is a monument depicting the [1968 Olympics Black Power salute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Olympics_Black_Power_salute "1968 Olympics Black Power salute") performed by African-American athletes [Tommie Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommie_Smith "Tommie Smith") and [John Carlos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carlos "John Carlos"). The monument consists of two [fiberglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiberglass "Fiberglass") statues covered in ceramic tiles, atop a concrete base designed to emulate the [Olympic podium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podium#Use_at_modern_Olympics "Podium"). It was created in 2005 by Portuguese artist [Rigo 23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigo_23 "Rigo 23") and is installed next to [Tower Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Hall_(San_Jose_State_University) "Tower Hall (San Jose State University)") on the [San José State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose_State_University "San Jose State University") campus, in [San Jose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose,_California "San Jose, California"), California, United States.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victory_Salute_(statue)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/John_Carlos%2C_Tommie_Smith%2C_Peter_Norman_1968cr.jpg/250px-John_Carlos%2C_Tommie_Smith%2C_Peter_Norman_1968cr.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Carlos,_Tommie_Smith,_Peter_Norman_1968cr.jpg)

The photo recreated by _Victory Salute_

In 1968, as members of San Jose State's [Speed City era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_City "Speed City") of athletics, Tommie Smith and John Carlos competed in the [1968 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Summer_Olympics "1968 Summer Olympics") in Mexico City. After earning gold and bronze medals respectively, the duo raised a [Black Power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Power "Black Power") salute while "[The Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Star-Spangled_Banner "The Star-Spangled Banner")" played, which became one of the most defining acts of protest of the [civil rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement "Civil rights movement").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-SJSU-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-BBC3-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-3) Despite disapproval of the protest among the general public, San Jose State University President [Robert D. Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_D._Clark "Robert D. Clark") expressed his support of the act.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-4)

In Winter 2002, San Jose State student Erik Grotz initiated a project to honor Smith and Carlos at their alma mater; "One of my professors [Cobie Harris][[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:5-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-6) was talking about unsung heroes and he mentioned Tommie Smith and John Carlos. He said these men had done a courageous thing to advance civil rights, and, yet, they had never been honored by their own school".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-7) Grotz worked with Department of Art Chair, Dr. Robert Milnes to create a mock-up to pitch to the university's Associated Students board, who approved the project on December 11, 2002, and began fundraising.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:0-8)

The Associated Students raised over $300,000 for the project[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-9)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:5-5) and initially intended the statue to be placed next to the now former location of the Scheller House[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-10) on the [Paseo de San Carlos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paseo_de_San_Carlos "Paseo de San Carlos").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-11) However, the project was moved to be on the lawn adjacent to the [Tower Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Hall_(San_Jose_State_University) "Tower Hall (San Jose State University)") and the Robert D. Clark Hall in order to be in a more central location on campus and to honor President Clark's support of the protest.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:4-12) On October 16, 2003, the 35th anniversary of the protest, Portuguese artist [Rigo 23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigo_23 "Rigo 23") was announced as the sculptor for the project.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:0-8)

_Victory Salute_ was assembled in early October 2005,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-13) and was unveiled to the public on October 17, 2005, drawing hundreds in attendance. A panel discussion was held featuring Smith and Carlos, as well as silver-medalist [Peter Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Norman "Peter Norman"), fellow Speed City era sprinter [Lee Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Evans_(sprinter) "Lee Evans (sprinter)"), and head coach [Payton Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payton_Jordan "Payton Jordan").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-14) Additional speeches were given by vice-mayor of San Jose [Cindy Chavez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cindy_Chavez "Cindy Chavez"), San Jose State President [Don W. Kassing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Kassing "Don Kassing"), and actor [Delroy Lindo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delroy_Lindo "Delroy Lindo"), followed by [honorary doctorate degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_degree "Honorary degree") awarded to Smith and Carlos.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:1-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-16) The statue was unveiled during a performance of "The Star-Spangled Banner", mirroring the original protest.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:1-15)

In January 2007, [History San Jose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_San_Jose "History San Jose") opened a new exhibit called _Speed City: From Civil Rights to Black Power_, covering the San Jose State athletic program. The exhibit focused on the San Jose State athletic program, highlighting how many student athletes from the Speed city program gained global recognition during Civil Rights and Black Power movements.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-17)

In 2008, after critics argued that _Victory Salute_ did not give unfamiliar onlookers the appropriate historical context, a plaque was added in front of the statue.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:3-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-19) The plaque reads:

> At the México City 1968 Olympic Games,  
> San José State University Student-Athletes   
> **Tommie Smith and John Carlos**  
> Stood for  
> **Justice, Dignity, Equality, and Peace.**  
>   
> Hereby the University and Associated Students  
> Commemorate their Legacy.   
>   
> October 16, 2005.[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/VictorySalutePlaque.jpg/250px-VictorySalutePlaque.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:VictorySalutePlaque.jpg)

Victory Salute plaque (2026)

In 2022, San Jose State students and faculty embedded _Victory Salute_ into their Public Art as Resistance project.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-22)

## Design

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victory_Salute_(statue)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Design")]

_Victory Salute_ was Rigo 23's first sculpture, but he wanted the statue to be a "labor of love". In order to correctly sculpt the musculature, he took [3D full-body scans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_scanning "3D scanning") of Smith and Carlos.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:4-12) Rigo 23's signature is on the back of Smith's shoe, and the year 2005 is on Carlos's shoe.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-23)

The statues' faces were rendered realistically and with emphasis placed on the emotion of the athletes. They were constructed from fiberglass over steel supports and covered with ceramic tiles, their track pants and jackets form a mosaic of dark blue ceramic tiles, with red and white detailing on the stripes of the track suits.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-24)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/PeterNormanPlaque.jpg/250px-PeterNormanPlaque.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PeterNormanPlaque.jpg)

Peter Norman's plaque (2026)

Peter Norman asked to be excluded from the monument, so that visitors could participate by standing in his place, and feeling what he felt.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-26) Norman said, "Anybody can get up there and stand up for something they believe in. I guess that just about says it all".[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-27)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:5-5) There is a plaque in the empty spot which reads "Fellow Athlete Australian Peter Norman Stood Here in Solidarity; Take a Stand".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:3-18)

## Use as protest space

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victory_Salute_(statue)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Use as protest space")]

Due to _Victory Salute_ depicting an act of protest during the civil rights movement, as well as its proximity to [San Jose City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose_City_Hall "San Jose City Hall") (less than 0.3 miles away), the statue and its surrounding lawn have been focal points for protests in San Jose.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-:3-18)

### 2020 Black Lives Matter protests

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victory_Salute_(statue)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2020 Black Lives Matter protests")]

On June 5, 2020, after the [murder of George Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_George_Floyd "Murder of George Floyd") and the ensuing [Black Lives Matter protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Black_Lives_Matter_protests "2020 Black Lives Matter protests"), a protest was held at _Victory Salute_ with protestors raising their fists, mirroring the 1968 protest.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-28) On September 1 of that year, [San Jose State student athletes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose_State_Spartans "San Jose State Spartans") organized a protest which started with the athletes giving speeches given at _Victory Salute_, followed by a march to the City Hall.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-29)

### 2024 pro-Palestine protests and encampment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victory_Salute_(statue)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2024 pro-Palestine protests and encampment")]

This section is an excerpt from [List of Gaza war protests at universities in California in 2024 § San José State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Gaza_war_protests_at_universities_in_California_in_2024#San_Jos%C3%A9_State "List of Gaza war protests at universities in California in 2024").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Gaza_war_protests_at_universities_in_California_in_2024&action=edit)]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Pro-Palestine_Protest_at_SJSU.jpg/250px-Pro-Palestine_Protest_at_SJSU.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pro-Palestine_Protest_at_SJSU.jpg)

The 2024 pro-Palestine encampment surrounding _Victory Salute_ at [San Jose State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose_State_University "San Jose State University")

On October 12, 2023, after the [Hamas-led attack on Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Hamas-led_attack_on_Israel "2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel") and subsequent [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war"), the [San Jose State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose_State_University "San Jose State University") chapter of [Students for Justice in Palestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Students_for_Justice_in_Palestine "Students for Justice in Palestine") organized a protest consisting of speeches given at _Victory Salute_, followed by a march around the campus.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-30)

In April 2024, following the [campus occupation at Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Columbia_University_pro-Palestinian_campus_occupation "2024 Columbia University pro-Palestinian campus occupation"), student protestors began demanding that San Jose State [divest from Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disinvestment_from_Israel "Disinvestment from Israel") over its [genocide of Palestinians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_genocide "Gaza genocide"). The university's Associated Students board unanimously adopted a measure to boycott [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley") companies involved in pro-Israeli activity on April 24.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-31)

Protests continued on campus,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-32) when on May 13, an encampment was established on the lawn around _Victory Salute_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-34) One of the encampment's demands was the firing of history professor Johnathan Roth after a physical altercation between himself and a pro-Palestine protestor in February 2024.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-36) On May 14, the University communicated with the protestors about their demands but asserted that the encampment had to be disbanded before finals began on May 15.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-38) Additionally, the University released a statement cosigned by _Victory Salute_'s subjects [Tommie Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommie_Smith "Tommie Smith"), and [John Carlos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carlos "John Carlos"), as well as by activist [Harry Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Edwards_(sociologist) "Harry Edwards (sociologist)"), and activist Ken Noel which expressed disapproval of the encampment around the statue.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-List_of_Gaza_war_protests_at_universities_in_California_in_2024_:22-39)_Victory Salute_'s artist, [Rigo 23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigo_23 "Rigo 23"), released a statement supporting the encampment and gave a speech at the encampment.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-List_of_Gaza_war_protests_at_universities_in_California_in_2024_:22-39)

On May 21, the protestors met with University President [Cynthia Teniente-Matson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Teniente-Matson "Cynthia Teniente-Matson") and Interim Vice President for Student Affairs Mari Fuentes-Martin to discuss the protestors' demands. Teniente-Matson suggested the creation of a student advisory council composed of students from Middle Eastern student organizations that would work with faculty to address concerns about university partnerships with Israel. Following these talks, the encampment was dismantled on May 23.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Salute_(statue)#cite_note-40)

## European Drug Report 2026

This year's European Drug Report 2026 is now available, presenting the latest evidence on drug use, supply, harms and responses across Europe. Based on data from 29 countries, this year’s report offers a comprehensive picture of Europe’s evolving drug landscape, with interactive visuals, open data and insights designed to support policy and practice.

This year's European Drug Report 2026 is now available, presenting the latest evidence on drug use, supply, harms and responses across Europe. Based on data from 29 countries, this year’s report offers a comprehensive picture of Europe’s evolving drug landscape, with interactive visuals, open data and insights designed to support policy and practice.

*   Bibliography

The statuette was found in 1888 between the Parthenon and the Sanctuary of Pandion. It portrays a long jump athlete who stands naked, projecting his left leg. His arms, bent at the elbows, stretch out in the front with his fists tightly closed as he would have held halters in them. His body posture shows the race, in which he participates, has just started. His muscular physique indicates that he is well-trained and his face is very expressive with symmetrical features. His short hair is folded in the form of a wreath over his forehead and nape.

The figurine must have been dedicated at the Acropolis sanctuary by one of the long jump athletes after his victory, most possibly in one of the contests held during the Panathenaia celebrations.

## Statuette of an athlete

Inventory number

ΕΑΜ Χ 6445

Category

Bronzes

Period

Archaic Period

Date

Around 500 BC

Dimensions

Height: 0.27 m

Material

Bronze

Location

First Floor Case 16, Νο 2

*   Description
*   Bibliography

The statuette was found in 1888 between the Parthenon and the Sanctuary of Pandion. It portrays a long jump athlete who stands naked, projecting his left leg. His arms, bent at the elbows, stretch out in the front with his fists tightly closed as he would have held halters in them. His body posture shows the race, in which he participates, has just started. His muscular physique indicates that he is well-trained and his face is very expressive with symmetrical features. His short hair is folded in the form of a wreath over his forehead and nape.

The figurine must have been dedicated at the Acropolis sanctuary by one of the long jump athletes after his victory, most possibly in one of the contests held during the Panathenaia celebrations.

# "Shoddy And Lousy": Kenyan Town Removes Athlete Statues After Uproar Online

## One particular statue that faced ridicule depicted a woman athlete running while holding a miniature Kenyan flag in her left hand.

*   Edited by: [Bhavya Sukheja](https://www.ndtv.com/authors/bhavya-sukheja-5856)
*   [World News](https://www.ndtv.com/world-news)
*   Aug 16, 2024 16:54 IST

    *   Published On Aug 16, 2024 16:49 IST  
    *   Last Updated On Aug 16, 2024 16:54 IST  

Read Time: 2 mins

![Image 2: "Shoddy And Lousy": Kenyan Town Removes Athlete Statues After Uproar Online](https://c.ndtvimg.com/2024-08/igf1bj38_kenya-statue_625x300_16_August_24.jpeg?downsize=773:435)

The pictures of the statues attracted uproar on social media.

Authorities in the Kenyan city of Eldoret have removed the statues of three athletes after they were widely ridiculed and described as shoddy. According to [_The Guardian_](https://www.theguardian.com/world/article/2024/aug/15/a-violation-kenyan-town-removes-athlete-statues-after-uproar-about-unrecognisable-features), the statues were unveiled earlier this week to showcase the town's agricultural and sports heritage. The sculptures included statues of athletes and one of a maize cob next to a wheat stalk. However, the pictures of the statues attracted uproar on social media. Local residents and Kenyans poked fun at the statues online and criticised the town's administration and sculptors.

One particular statue that faced ridicule depicted a woman athlete running while holding a miniature Kenyan flag in her left hand. Sharing the picture of the statue on X (formerly Twitter), one user said that the works represented "our collective mediocrity as a country". "Eldoret City launch. Who is this? This is a violation," wrote another user. "This is shoddy and lousy to say the least. We can do better than this," commented a third.

> These statue of Faith Kipyegon and Eliud Kipchoge in Eldoret represent our collective mediocrity as a country. [pic.twitter.com/R9BLlbisAm](https://t.co/R9BLlbisAm)
> 
> — Gwalla (@its_Edwin0) [August 15, 2024](https://twitter.com/its_Edwin0/status/1823960671450476591?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Another statue that caught the attention of social media users was of marathon legend Eliud Kipchoge. One user shared a picture of the sculpture and described it as a "joke". "Whoever did this will not see heaven," the user wrote.

> [#MainaAndKingangi](https://twitter.com/hashtag/MainaAndKingangi?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)[@ItsMainaKageni](https://twitter.com/ItsMainaKageni?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)[@Classic105Kenya](https://twitter.com/Classic105Kenya?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)  
> Kenya is a Joke  
> Whoever did this to our Athletes will not see Heaven  
> Alaaaa  
> Kipchoge Statue in US VS KENYA [pic.twitter.com/GVKa2Cnken](https://t.co/GVKa2Cnken)
> 
> — KIPLETING MANUELA SON OF ELDORET (@ItsKipleting) [August 15, 2024](https://twitter.com/ItsKipleting/status/1823959810238202242?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

After criticism, authorities in the Kenyan city removed the sculptures at night. The [_BBC_](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cwyxd93w4y2o)reported that the county official removed three statues - two representing female athletes and one of a male. All the sculptures have been taken to an unknown location, officials said.

Kenyans online welcomed the removal of the status. It is not clear whether the sculptures would be replaced, or when.

Meanwhile, Eldoret was conferred city status earlier this week. At the same time, Kenyan President William Ruto honoured Kenyan medalists from the Paris Olympics at an event at Eldoret state lodge. The athletes later had an open-car parade, attracting cheers from thousands of residents who lined the city's streets to celebrate them.

Kenya was the highest-ranked African country at the Paris Olympics, coming 17th on the medal table with four golds, two silver and five bronze medals.

# "Shoddy And Lousy": Kenyan Town Removes Athlete Statues After Uproar Online

## One particular statue that faced ridicule depicted a woman athlete running while holding a miniature Kenyan flag in her left hand.

*   Edited by: [Bhavya Sukheja](https://www.ndtv.com/authors/bhavya-sukheja-5856)

![Image 2: "Shoddy And Lousy": Kenyan Town Removes Athlete Statues After Uproar Online](https://c.ndtvimg.com/2024-08/igf1bj38_kenya-statue_625x300_16_August_24.jpeg?downsize=773:435)

The pictures of the statues attracted uproar on social media.

Authorities in the Kenyan city of Eldoret have removed the statues of three athletes after they were widely ridiculed and described as shoddy. According to [_The Guardian_](https://www.theguardian.com/world/article/2024/aug/15/a-violation-kenyan-town-removes-athlete-statues-after-uproar-about-unrecognisable-features), the statues were unveiled earlier this week to showcase the town's agricultural and sports heritage. The sculptures included statues of athletes and one of a maize cob next to a wheat stalk. However, the pictures of the statues attracted uproar on social media. Local residents and Kenyans poked fun at the statues online and criticised the town's administration and sculptors.

One particular statue that faced ridicule depicted a woman athlete running while holding a miniature Kenyan flag in her left hand. Sharing the picture of the statue on X (formerly Twitter), one user said that the works represented "our collective mediocrity as a country". "Eldoret City launch. Who is this? This is a violation," wrote another user. "This is shoddy and lousy to say the least. We can do better than this," commented a third.

> These statue of Faith Kipyegon and Eliud Kipchoge in Eldoret represent our collective mediocrity as a country. [pic.twitter.com/R9BLlbisAm](https://t.co/R9BLlbisAm)
> 
> — Gwalla (@its_Edwin0) [August 15, 2024](https://twitter.com/its_Edwin0/status/1823960671450476591?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Another statue that caught the attention of social media users was of marathon legend Eliud Kipchoge. One user shared a picture of the sculpture and described it as a "joke". "Whoever did this will not see heaven," the user wrote.

> [#MainaAndKingangi](https://twitter.com/hashtag/MainaAndKingangi?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)[@ItsMainaKageni](https://twitter.com/ItsMainaKageni?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)[@Classic105Kenya](https://twitter.com/Classic105Kenya?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)  
> Kenya is a Joke  
> Whoever did this to our Athletes will not see Heaven  
> Alaaaa  
> Kipchoge Statue in US VS KENYA [pic.twitter.com/GVKa2Cnken](https://t.co/GVKa2Cnken)
> 
> — KIPLETING MANUELA SON OF ELDORET (@ItsKipleting) [August 15, 2024](https://twitter.com/ItsKipleting/status/1823959810238202242?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

After criticism, authorities in the Kenyan city removed the sculptures at night. The [_BBC_](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cwyxd93w4y2o)reported that the county official removed three statues - two representing female athletes and one of a male. All the sculptures have been taken to an unknown location, officials said.

Kenyans online welcomed the removal of the status. It is not clear whether the sculptures would be replaced, or when.

Meanwhile, Eldoret was conferred city status earlier this week. At the same time, Kenyan President William Ruto honoured Kenyan medalists from the Paris Olympics at an event at Eldoret state lodge. The athletes later had an open-car parade, attracting cheers from thousands of residents who lined the city's streets to celebrate them.

Kenya was the highest-ranked African country at the Paris Olympics, coming 17th on the medal table with four golds, two silver and five bronze medals.

### Description

This idealized athlete recalls Greek sculptural types invented and popularized during the 400s BC. Large-scale athletes and other sculptures like this were originally created by famous artists as sanctuary dedications. Centuries later, they were widely copied and adapted by Roman sculptors, whose clients sought their own versions of earlier masterpieces. Working in marble rather than bronze, these sculptors added certain elements for stability, such as the struts and the large tree trunk beside the right leg here. Sculptures like this one are profoundly complex, made by and for Romans but descended from Greek ancestors.

### Description

This idealized athlete recalls Greek sculptural types invented and popularized during the 400s BC. Large-scale athletes and other sculptures like this were originally created by famous artists as sanctuary dedications. Centuries later, they were widely copied and adapted by Roman sculptors, whose clients sought their own versions of earlier masterpieces. Working in marble rather than bronze, these sculptors added certain elements for stability, such as the struts and the large tree trunk beside the right leg here. Sculptures like this one are profoundly complex, made by and for Romans but descended from Greek ancestors.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Bronze_casting_by_the_Lost_Wax_Method.png/250px-Bronze_casting_by_the_Lost_Wax_Method.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bronze_casting_by_the_Lost_Wax_Method.png)

The lost wax technique

The _**Victorious Youth**_, also known as the _**Atleta di Fano**_, the _**Lisippo di Fano**_ or the _**Getty Bronze**_, is a [Greek bronze sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_sculpture "Ancient Greek sculpture"), made between 300 and 100 BCE,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-guardian-giuffrida2-1) in the collections of the [J. Paul Getty Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Paul_Getty_Museum "J. Paul Getty Museum"), displayed at the [Getty Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getty_Villa "Getty Villa") in [Pacific Palisades, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Palisades,_California "Pacific Palisades, California").

The _Victorious Youth_ was found in the summer of 1964 in the sea off [Fano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fano "Fano") on the [Adriatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriatic_Sea "Adriatic Sea") coast of Italy, snagged in the nets of an Italian [fishing trawler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing_trawler "Fishing trawler"). In the summer of 1977, the J. Paul Getty Museum purchased the bronze. [Bernard Ashmole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Ashmole "Bernard Ashmole"), an archaeologist and art historian, was asked to inspect the sculpture by Munich [art dealer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_dealer "Art dealer") Heinz Herzer; he and other scholars attributed it to [Lysippos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysippos "Lysippos"), a prolific sculptor of Classical Greek art. The research and conservation of the _Victorious Youth_ dates from the 1980s to the 1990s and is based on studies in classical bronzes by ancient Mediterranean specialists in collaboration with the Getty Museum.

The entire sculpture was cast in one piece through a casting technique called the [lost wax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost-wax_casting "Lost-wax casting") method: the sculpture was first created in clay with support to allow hot air to melt the wax, creating a mold for molten bronze to be poured into and making the large bronze _Victorious Youth_.

More recently, scholars have been concerned with the original social context, such as where the sculpture was made, for what context and who the subject might be. Multiple interpretations of where the _Youth_ was made and who the _Youth_ is are expressed in scholarly books by [Jiri Frel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ji%C5%99%C3%AD_Frel "Jiří Frel"), J Paul Getty Museum curator from 1973 to 1986, and [Carol Mattusch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Mattusch "Carol Mattusch"), professor of art history at [George Mason University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mason_University "George Mason University") specializing in Greek and Roman art with a focus on classical bronzes.

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]

The sculpture may have been part of the crowd of sculptures of victorious athletes at Panhellenic Greek sanctuaries like [Delphi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi "Delphi") and [Olympia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympia,_Greece "Olympia, Greece"). Analysis of fibres from the core revealed that they are [flax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flax "Flax"); [Pausanias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pausanias_(geographer) "Pausanias (geographer)") noted in the second century CE that the only flax being grown in Greece was to be found around Olympia. Other research has developed an argument that the _Bronze_ represents a victorious athlete and a young prince whose lineage relates to [Alexander the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2) Therefore, this Olympic statue might have been dedicated anywhere within the ancient Greek world rather than Delphi or Olympia.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2)

A possible reconstruction of the _Victorious Youth_ is that the statue could have held a palm frond, as these were gifts given to the victors. His right hand reaches to touch the winner's [olive wreath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olive_wreath "Olive wreath") on his head. The powerful head has led the _Victorious Youth_ conservators to see it as a portrait; X-rays suggest that the head was cast separately. With this technique the artist is able to focus on the head as an individual project to the full composition of the lithe body. The athlete's eyes were once inlaid, probably with bone, and his nipples are in contrasting copper. In addition to the wreath, the statue's build gives clues as to the subject: this individual is a slender young man with a confident gaze, but nothing about him refers to strength; his body is not particularly muscular or powerful in its stance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:14-3)

## Techniques

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Techniques")]

### The lost wax process

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The lost wax process")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/L%27atleta_di_Fano.jpg/250px-L%27atleta_di_Fano.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:L'atleta_di_Fano.jpg)

The bronze _Victorious Youth_ at the Getty Museum. Height: 1.52 metres (5 feet) without lower legs and feet.

Like many other Greek artworks, the bronze statue was made through the lost wax method. Initially, the artist created an armature or support made with a thick wooden stick, iron bars or wires, and ancient reed sticks to support appendages from the torso. Surrounding the armature was a mixture of loam, sand, pebbles, pistachio nuts, fragments of clay and ivory, and glue. This combination kept the structure stable through multiple layers of application. After the final layer of clay was applied, wax sheets covered the statue's surface. During this process wax plates supported the figure from multiple points holding the statue vertically. Nails pierced into the wax to the inner core and protruded outwards to keep the statue positioned with the external mold. Slow heating allowed the wax to melt and fired the center and mold into a stable position. As the wax melted, an air space formed, creating a mold of the _Victorious Youth_, which became filled with molten bronze. The entire sculpture was cast in one piece.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2)

### Polychromy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Polychromy")]

Evidence of [polychrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polychrome "Polychrome") survives; the nipples and lips are copper. This color choice may have interacted with the golden yellow of the bronze surface. There is a possibility of silver on the olive crown and more color to enhance the cheeks.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2) The inserted eyes would have given the bronze statue a naturalistic look. During the casting process of the _Youth_, these eye sockets would have been left empty and after the casting process both eyes would be inserted. The iris and pupil would be made of stone or glass; the whites of the eyes would be ivory, bone or glass. To hold the eye in place a reddish sheet of copper would have been cut to fit the eye socket and then be curled into lashes. In addition to the application of bone, copper, glass, ivory, the bronze would be painted pale and gleaming like flesh to its viewers of the ancient world.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-4)

## Attribution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Attribution")]

In the late 1980s antiquity scholars and Getty Museum curator Jiri Frel used [radiocarbon dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiocarbon_dating "Radiocarbon dating") and stylistic analysis to attribute the _Youth_ to Lysippos. Using [Polykleitos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polykleitos "Polykleitos")'s statues as a comparison, scholars see a change from _Polykleitan Kanon_: the proportions become more subtle and richer in detail. There is a shift from the squareness in the face and innovative applications of elongation in the details of face and body. Lysippos was praised for his ability to evoke the soul from his statues through fleeting expressions.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-5) Establishing an exact artist for the work is challenging due to the lack of original Greek bronzes to use for comparison. Ancient literature gives testimony of the classical sculptors; however, the artist did not sign the statues. There is no physical evidence to support the conclusion that Lysippos was the sculptor, but Frel, Mattusch, and ancient literary source [Pliny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Elder "Pliny the Elder") theorize that Lysippos or his student was the _Youth's_ creator. In Pliny's [_Natural History_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_History_(Pliny) "Natural History (Pliny)"), he includes information about Greek sculptors extracted from earlier texts that are lost to us. During the fourth century BCE, Lysippos produced a multitude of sculptures; he alone probably sculpted fifteen hundred statues. He came from a family of bronze workers who developed a new method of increasing production, and statues of athletes were a specialty.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:14-3)

## Dating

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Dating")]

### Origin

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Origin")]

In 1974, Jerry Podany, antiquities conservator at the Getty Museum, and Marie Svoboda, a post-graduate intern in antiquities conservation at the Museum, radiocarbon-dated a piece of wood that came from the statue's core, establishing the bronze as an ancient piece of work.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-6) Over one month, conservator Rudolph Stapp removed the core of the bronze to eliminate issues related to humidity. During the removal, thermoluminescence dating and carbon-14 methods confirmed the dating of the _Victorious Youth_ to pre-Roman times. The rectangular plate on the statue's back of neck functioned as support for the _Bronze's_ vertical position, a technique shared by two other fourth-century bronzes: the _[Marathon Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon\_Boy "Marathon Boy")_ and the _[Antikythera Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera\_Ephebe "Antikythera Ephebe")_. The curved body, raised hip, and smooth and youthful anatomy are characteristics of a universal style—the fifth century BCE developed these frameworks as a canonical expression of classical values. This form of expression went on through two and a half millennia, making dating and attribution challenging to determine with confidence. Despite slightly different interpretations, a collective agreement states that production can be dated to between the late fourth century and middle of the third century BCE.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:14-3)

### Collectors in antiquity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Collectors in antiquity")]

Many statues from Greek cities and sanctuaries moved into Roman possession by the second century BCE. Vast collections of the antique style flourished, various statuary were looted and repurposed for Roman decoration. Like many other bronzes, the _Victorious Youth_ traveled across the Mediterranean on its way to Italy for reinstallation, possibly in public areas or in private homes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:14-3)

## Interpretation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Interpretation")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Surviving_Greek_Bronze.jpg/250px-Surviving_Greek_Bronze.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Surviving_Greek_Bronze.jpg)

_Victorious Youth_

According to Jiri Frel, the stance and proportion of the "_Getty Bronze"_ (Frel's name for the statue) are similar to those of Lysippos's portrait of [Demetrios Poliorketes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demetrius_I_of_Macedon "Demetrius I of Macedon") (336–283 BCE).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2) The least controversial theory is that the strong calves emphasize his athletic abilities, making him an Olympic runner who held a victor's palm branch in his left arm.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-7) Claims state there are actual traces of palm after studying the statue.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-8) Interpreting the anatomy is important in identifying the statue, from the detail in the joints, delicate attention to the wrists and ends of fingers there is a youthful representation. Greek games functioned as a major aspect in Greek culture and art. During the second century CE, athletic contests were consistent events in various cities throughout Greece. At Olympia, these games were categorized for men, youths and boys. The [Panhellenic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panhellenic_Games "Panhellenic Games") occurred at religious sanctuaries in honor of the gods; [Delphi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi "Delphi") hosted [Pythian games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythian_Games "Pythian Games") as gifts for Apollo and athletic events at [Olympia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Zeus,_Olympia "Temple of Zeus, Olympia") honored Zeus. These games included footraces, combat sports, pentathlon, horse racing, and [chariot racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chariot_racing "Chariot racing"). Delphi involved singing and playing of instruments in these Panhellenic Games. The victors received wreaths of different leaves depending on the site location: laurel at Delphi, olive at Olympia, pine at [Isthmia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isthmian_Games "Isthmian Games"), and wild celery at Nemea.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2) By understanding the specific wreaths worn by the winners, one could hypothesize which temple the statue would have housed.

Jiri Frel in 1982 examined the statue and associated it with Alexander the Great, based on the stance and other features representing not just a well-bred citizen but one higher in class. The artist's ability to not only capture beauty but produce a work of art that emphasizes the classical structures of Greek art during the Hellenistic period suggests the _Youth_ as a member of one of the royal families descended from Alexander.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-9) However, this theory did not survive the criticism of other scholars. Not until the 1990s was the next attempt made to identify the sculpture, and the Getty Museum did not approve the suggested name. Now much debate and research is specific to anatomy, date and authorship, but with the uncertainties of stylistic assessments it is difficult to reach a consensus.

## Discovery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Discovery")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Statue_of_a_Victorious_Youth%2C_pre-conservation_-_Getty_Museum_%2877.AB.30%29.jpg/250px-Statue_of_a_Victorious_Youth%2C_pre-conservation_-_Getty_Museum_%2877.AB.30%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Statue_of_a_Victorious_Youth,_pre-conservation_-_Getty_Museum_(77.AB.30).jpg)

The _Victorious Youth_ before restoration

Classical Greek and Roman sculptures have been found in various parts of the Mediterranean; both Greek and Roman settlements existed in the Iberian Peninsula, on Africa's northern coast, in Asia Minor, the Middle East, and modern-day Europe. Many underwater bronzes have been discovered along the Aegean and Mediterranean coasts. Sponge divers found the _[Antikythera Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera\_Ephebe "Antikythera Ephebe")_ and the _Portrait Head of a [Stoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoicism "Stoicism")_ at Antikythera in 1900. Other well-known underwater bronze finds include those from the [Mahdia shipwreck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahdia_shipwreck "Mahdia shipwreck") off the coast of Tunisia, 1907; the _[Marathon Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon\_Boy "Marathon Boy")_ off the coast of Marathon, 1925; the standing _[Artemision Bronze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemision\_Bronze "Artemision Bronze")_ of Zeus or Poseidon found off Cape Artemision in northern Euboea, 1926; the _[Jockey of Artemision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jockey\_of\_Artemision "Jockey of Artemision")_ found off Cape Artemision, 1928 and 1937; the [Riace bronzes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riace_bronzes "Riace bronzes"), 1972; the _[Dancing Satyr of Mazara del Vallo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing\_Satyr\_of\_Mazara\_del\_Vallo "Dancing Satyr of Mazara del Vallo")_ near Brindisi, 1992; and the _[Apoxyomenos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apoxyomenos "Apoxyomenos")_ off the [Croatian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatia "Croatia") island of [Lošinj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lo%C5%A1inj "Lošinj"), 1999.

The _Victorious Youth_ was found in the summer of 1964 in the sea off [Fano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fano "Fano") on the [Adriatic coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriatic_Sea "Adriatic Sea") of Italy, snagged in the nets of an Italian fishing trawler, the _Ferri Ferruccio_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-10) Italian art dealers paid the fishermen US$5,600 for it.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-guardian-giuffrida2-1) The Getty Museum bought it from German art dealer Herman Heinz Herzer for almost US$4 million in 1977.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-guardian-giuffrida2-1) Before conservation, a thick layer of encrustation covered the statue, suggesting it has been immersed since antiquity, rather than as a result of medieval or late Venetian ships transporting the object as spoils of war or recycling it for scrap metal.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-11)

The precise location of the shipwreck, which preserved this object from being melted down like all but a tiny fraction of Greek bronzes, has not been established; it seems most likely that a [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome") ship carrying looted objects was on its way to [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy") when it sank. The statue has been roughly broken off its former base, breaking away at the ankles. The clay core inside may give further detail to where and when it was made.

## Restoration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Restoration")]

In 1972 Heinz Herzer and Volker Kinnius, the Munich gallery owner, wrote a report on the conservation project of Rudolph Stapp.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-12) Stapp, known for his specialty in ancient bronzes, was the main conservationist working on the _Victorious Youth_. Past efforts to remove encrustation from the _Bronze_ left scratches in the metal. The _Victorious Youth_ took three months to clean. First, the statue went into an artificial humidity chamber, exposing 'bronze disease'. This degradation occurs when chlorides and salts in the bronze react with moisture, producing discolored spots. If the condition is left untreated, the copper part of the bronze can easily be lost, leaving a disfigured image. The conservators neutralized the active corrosion by submerging it in a heated solution of sodium sesquicarbonate. The _Victorious Youth_ was then placed in a vacuum with the solution to penetrate interior layers without washing anything out. This process was repeated twice and was finalized with one last artificial humidity test to check for bronze disease resurfacing. An environment with a relative humidity under 35% is necessary to keep the statue from deteriorating.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2)

## Provenance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Provenance")]

After the bronze was retrieved in 1964 it was brought to land in Italy, where it reportedly passed through several hands on the black market.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-Kazmin,_FT_05022024-13) It emerged in 1971 under the ownership of the Artemis Consortium, an association of several international art dealers, and was then stored with a Munich art dealer, Heinz Herzer.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-14)

The [Getty Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getty_Museum "Getty Museum") is involved in a controversy regarding proper title to a number of the artwork in its collection. The Museum's previous curator of [antiquities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiquities "Antiquities"), [Marion True](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_True "Marion True"), was indicted in Italy in 2005 along with [Robert E. Hecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Hecht "Robert E. Hecht") on criminal charges relating to trafficking in stolen antiquities. The primary evidence in the case came from the 1995 raid of a [Geneva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva "Geneva"), [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland") warehouse that was found to contain stolen artifacts. Italian art dealer [Giacomo Medici](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Medici_(art_dealer) "Giacomo Medici (art dealer)") was eventually arrested in 1997; his operation was reported to be "one of the largest and most sophisticated antiquities networks in the world, responsible for illegally digging up and spiriting away thousands of top-drawer pieces and passing them on to the most elite end of the international art market".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-15) In a letter to the [J. Paul Getty Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Paul_Getty_Trust "J. Paul Getty Trust") on December 18, 2006, True stated that she was being made to "carry the burden" for practices that were known, approved, and condoned by the Getty's Board of Directors.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-16)

On November 20, 2006, the Director of the museum, [Michael Brand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Brand_(art_historian) "Michael Brand (art historian)"), announced that 26 disputed pieces were to be returned to [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"). These did not include the _Victorious Youth_, for which judicial proceedings were still pending. In an interview to the Italian national newspaper _[Corriere della Sera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corriere\_della\_Sera "Corriere della Sera")_ on December 20, 2006, the Italian Minister of Cultural Heritage declared that Italy would place the museum under a cultural embargo if all the 52 disputed pieces did not return to Italy. On August 1, 2007, an agreement was announced providing that the museum would return 40 pieces to Italy out of the 52 requested, among them the _Venus of Morgantina_, which was returned in 2010, but not the _Victorious Youth_, whose outcome depended upon the results of the criminal proceedings in Italy. On that same day the public prosecutor of Pesaro formally requested that the statue be confiscated as it was unlawfully exported out of Italy, giving rise to a dispute that came before the Constitutional Court.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-17)

Among the arguments the Getty advanced for retaining the sculpture were that, although the sculpture was retrieved by an Italian vessel, it was found in international, not Italian, waters and that it is not the work of an Italian but a Greek artist.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-Kazmin,_FT_05022024-13) However, on November 30, 2018, the [Supreme Court of Cassation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Cassation_(Italy) "Supreme Court of Cassation (Italy)") denied an appeal by the Getty Museum, affirming that Italy has a right to reclaim the _Victorious Youth_.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-18) On May 2, 2024, the [European Court of Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Court_of_Human_Rights "European Court of Human Rights") affirmed the ruling of Italy's Supreme Court of Cassation.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-19)

The _**Victorious Youth**_, also known as the _**Atleta di Fano**_, the _**Lisippo di Fano**_ or the _**Getty Bronze**_, is a [Greek bronze sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_sculpture "Ancient Greek sculpture"), made between 300 and 100 BCE,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-guardian-giuffrida2-1) in the collections of the [J. Paul Getty Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Paul_Getty_Museum "J. Paul Getty Museum"), displayed at the [Getty Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getty_Villa "Getty Villa") in [Pacific Palisades, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Palisades,_California "Pacific Palisades, California").

The _Victorious Youth_ was found in the summer of 1964 in the sea off [Fano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fano "Fano") on the [Adriatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriatic_Sea "Adriatic Sea") coast of Italy, snagged in the nets of an Italian [fishing trawler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing_trawler "Fishing trawler"). In the summer of 1977, the J. Paul Getty Museum purchased the bronze. [Bernard Ashmole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Ashmole "Bernard Ashmole"), an archaeologist and art historian, was asked to inspect the sculpture by Munich [art dealer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_dealer "Art dealer") Heinz Herzer; he and other scholars attributed it to [Lysippos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysippos "Lysippos"), a prolific sculptor of Classical Greek art. The research and conservation of the _Victorious Youth_ dates from the 1980s to the 1990s and is based on studies in classical bronzes by ancient Mediterranean specialists in collaboration with the Getty Museum.

The entire sculpture was cast in one piece through a casting technique called the [lost wax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost-wax_casting "Lost-wax casting") method: the sculpture was first created in clay with support to allow hot air to melt the wax, creating a mold for molten bronze to be poured into and making the large bronze _Victorious Youth_.

More recently, scholars have been concerned with the original social context, such as where the sculpture was made, for what context and who the subject might be. Multiple interpretations of where the _Youth_ was made and who the _Youth_ is are expressed in scholarly books by [Jiri Frel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ji%C5%99%C3%AD_Frel "Jiří Frel"), J Paul Getty Museum curator from 1973 to 1986, and [Carol Mattusch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Mattusch "Carol Mattusch"), professor of art history at [George Mason University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mason_University "George Mason University") specializing in Greek and Roman art with a focus on classical bronzes.

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]

The sculpture may have been part of the crowd of sculptures of victorious athletes at Panhellenic Greek sanctuaries like [Delphi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi "Delphi") and [Olympia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympia,_Greece "Olympia, Greece"). Analysis of fibres from the core revealed that they are [flax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flax "Flax"); [Pausanias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pausanias_(geographer) "Pausanias (geographer)") noted in the second century CE that the only flax being grown in Greece was to be found around Olympia. Other research has developed an argument that the _Bronze_ represents a victorious athlete and a young prince whose lineage relates to [Alexander the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2) Therefore, this Olympic statue might have been dedicated anywhere within the ancient Greek world rather than Delphi or Olympia.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2)

A possible reconstruction of the _Victorious Youth_ is that the statue could have held a palm frond, as these were gifts given to the victors. His right hand reaches to touch the winner's [olive wreath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olive_wreath "Olive wreath") on his head. The powerful head has led the _Victorious Youth_ conservators to see it as a portrait; X-rays suggest that the head was cast separately. With this technique the artist is able to focus on the head as an individual project to the full composition of the lithe body. The athlete's eyes were once inlaid, probably with bone, and his nipples are in contrasting copper. In addition to the wreath, the statue's build gives clues as to the subject: this individual is a slender young man with a confident gaze, but nothing about him refers to strength; his body is not particularly muscular or powerful in its stance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:14-3)

## Techniques

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Techniques")]

### The lost wax process

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The lost wax process")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/L%27atleta_di_Fano.jpg/250px-L%27atleta_di_Fano.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:L'atleta_di_Fano.jpg)

The bronze _Victorious Youth_ at the Getty Museum. Height: 1.52 metres (5 feet) without lower legs and feet.

Like many other Greek artworks, the bronze statue was made through the lost wax method. Initially, the artist created an armature or support made with a thick wooden stick, iron bars or wires, and ancient reed sticks to support appendages from the torso. Surrounding the armature was a mixture of loam, sand, pebbles, pistachio nuts, fragments of clay and ivory, and glue. This combination kept the structure stable through multiple layers of application. After the final layer of clay was applied, wax sheets covered the statue's surface. During this process wax plates supported the figure from multiple points holding the statue vertically. Nails pierced into the wax to the inner core and protruded outwards to keep the statue positioned with the external mold. Slow heating allowed the wax to melt and fired the center and mold into a stable position. As the wax melted, an air space formed, creating a mold of the _Victorious Youth_, which became filled with molten bronze. The entire sculpture was cast in one piece.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2)

### Polychromy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Polychromy")]

Evidence of [polychrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polychrome "Polychrome") survives; the nipples and lips are copper. This color choice may have interacted with the golden yellow of the bronze surface. There is a possibility of silver on the olive crown and more color to enhance the cheeks.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2) The inserted eyes would have given the bronze statue a naturalistic look. During the casting process of the _Youth_, these eye sockets would have been left empty and after the casting process both eyes would be inserted. The iris and pupil would be made of stone or glass; the whites of the eyes would be ivory, bone or glass. To hold the eye in place a reddish sheet of copper would have been cut to fit the eye socket and then be curled into lashes. In addition to the application of bone, copper, glass, ivory, the bronze would be painted pale and gleaming like flesh to its viewers of the ancient world.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-4)

## Attribution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Attribution")]

In the late 1980s antiquity scholars and Getty Museum curator Jiri Frel used [radiocarbon dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiocarbon_dating "Radiocarbon dating") and stylistic analysis to attribute the _Youth_ to Lysippos. Using [Polykleitos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polykleitos "Polykleitos")'s statues as a comparison, scholars see a change from _Polykleitan Kanon_: the proportions become more subtle and richer in detail. There is a shift from the squareness in the face and innovative applications of elongation in the details of face and body. Lysippos was praised for his ability to evoke the soul from his statues through fleeting expressions.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-5) Establishing an exact artist for the work is challenging due to the lack of original Greek bronzes to use for comparison. Ancient literature gives testimony of the classical sculptors; however, the artist did not sign the statues. There is no physical evidence to support the conclusion that Lysippos was the sculptor, but Frel, Mattusch, and ancient literary source [Pliny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Elder "Pliny the Elder") theorize that Lysippos or his student was the _Youth's_ creator. In Pliny's [_Natural History_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_History_(Pliny) "Natural History (Pliny)"), he includes information about Greek sculptors extracted from earlier texts that are lost to us. During the fourth century BCE, Lysippos produced a multitude of sculptures; he alone probably sculpted fifteen hundred statues. He came from a family of bronze workers who developed a new method of increasing production, and statues of athletes were a specialty.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:14-3)

## Dating

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Dating")]

### Origin

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Origin")]

In 1974, Jerry Podany, antiquities conservator at the Getty Museum, and Marie Svoboda, a post-graduate intern in antiquities conservation at the Museum, radiocarbon-dated a piece of wood that came from the statue's core, establishing the bronze as an ancient piece of work.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-6) Over one month, conservator Rudolph Stapp removed the core of the bronze to eliminate issues related to humidity. During the removal, thermoluminescence dating and carbon-14 methods confirmed the dating of the _Victorious Youth_ to pre-Roman times. The rectangular plate on the statue's back of neck functioned as support for the _Bronze's_ vertical position, a technique shared by two other fourth-century bronzes: the _[Marathon Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon\_Boy "Marathon Boy")_ and the _[Antikythera Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera\_Ephebe "Antikythera Ephebe")_. The curved body, raised hip, and smooth and youthful anatomy are characteristics of a universal style—the fifth century BCE developed these frameworks as a canonical expression of classical values. This form of expression went on through two and a half millennia, making dating and attribution challenging to determine with confidence. Despite slightly different interpretations, a collective agreement states that production can be dated to between the late fourth century and middle of the third century BCE.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:14-3)

### Collectors in antiquity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Collectors in antiquity")]

Many statues from Greek cities and sanctuaries moved into Roman possession by the second century BCE. Vast collections of the antique style flourished, various statuary were looted and repurposed for Roman decoration. Like many other bronzes, the _Victorious Youth_ traveled across the Mediterranean on its way to Italy for reinstallation, possibly in public areas or in private homes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:14-3)

## Interpretation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Interpretation")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Surviving_Greek_Bronze.jpg/250px-Surviving_Greek_Bronze.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Surviving_Greek_Bronze.jpg)

_Victorious Youth_

According to Jiri Frel, the stance and proportion of the "_Getty Bronze"_ (Frel's name for the statue) are similar to those of Lysippos's portrait of [Demetrios Poliorketes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demetrius_I_of_Macedon "Demetrius I of Macedon") (336–283 BCE).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2) The least controversial theory is that the strong calves emphasize his athletic abilities, making him an Olympic runner who held a victor's palm branch in his left arm.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-7) Claims state there are actual traces of palm after studying the statue.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-8) Interpreting the anatomy is important in identifying the statue, from the detail in the joints, delicate attention to the wrists and ends of fingers there is a youthful representation. Greek games functioned as a major aspect in Greek culture and art. During the second century CE, athletic contests were consistent events in various cities throughout Greece. At Olympia, these games were categorized for men, youths and boys. The [Panhellenic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panhellenic_Games "Panhellenic Games") occurred at religious sanctuaries in honor of the gods; [Delphi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi "Delphi") hosted [Pythian games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythian_Games "Pythian Games") as gifts for Apollo and athletic events at [Olympia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Zeus,_Olympia "Temple of Zeus, Olympia") honored Zeus. These games included footraces, combat sports, pentathlon, horse racing, and [chariot racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chariot_racing "Chariot racing"). Delphi involved singing and playing of instruments in these Panhellenic Games. The victors received wreaths of different leaves depending on the site location: laurel at Delphi, olive at Olympia, pine at [Isthmia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isthmian_Games "Isthmian Games"), and wild celery at Nemea.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2) By understanding the specific wreaths worn by the winners, one could hypothesize which temple the statue would have housed.

Jiri Frel in 1982 examined the statue and associated it with Alexander the Great, based on the stance and other features representing not just a well-bred citizen but one higher in class. The artist's ability to not only capture beauty but produce a work of art that emphasizes the classical structures of Greek art during the Hellenistic period suggests the _Youth_ as a member of one of the royal families descended from Alexander.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-9) However, this theory did not survive the criticism of other scholars. Not until the 1990s was the next attempt made to identify the sculpture, and the Getty Museum did not approve the suggested name. Now much debate and research is specific to anatomy, date and authorship, but with the uncertainties of stylistic assessments it is difficult to reach a consensus.

## Discovery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Discovery")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Statue_of_a_Victorious_Youth%2C_pre-conservation_-_Getty_Museum_%2877.AB.30%29.jpg/250px-Statue_of_a_Victorious_Youth%2C_pre-conservation_-_Getty_Museum_%2877.AB.30%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Statue_of_a_Victorious_Youth,_pre-conservation_-_Getty_Museum_(77.AB.30).jpg)

The _Victorious Youth_ before restoration

Classical Greek and Roman sculptures have been found in various parts of the Mediterranean; both Greek and Roman settlements existed in the Iberian Peninsula, on Africa's northern coast, in Asia Minor, the Middle East, and modern-day Europe. Many underwater bronzes have been discovered along the Aegean and Mediterranean coasts. Sponge divers found the _[Antikythera Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera\_Ephebe "Antikythera Ephebe")_ and the _Portrait Head of a [Stoic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoicism "Stoicism")_ at Antikythera in 1900. Other well-known underwater bronze finds include those from the [Mahdia shipwreck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahdia_shipwreck "Mahdia shipwreck") off the coast of Tunisia, 1907; the _[Marathon Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon\_Boy "Marathon Boy")_ off the coast of Marathon, 1925; the standing _[Artemision Bronze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemision\_Bronze "Artemision Bronze")_ of Zeus or Poseidon found off Cape Artemision in northern Euboea, 1926; the _[Jockey of Artemision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jockey\_of\_Artemision "Jockey of Artemision")_ found off Cape Artemision, 1928 and 1937; the [Riace bronzes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riace_bronzes "Riace bronzes"), 1972; the _[Dancing Satyr of Mazara del Vallo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing\_Satyr\_of\_Mazara\_del\_Vallo "Dancing Satyr of Mazara del Vallo")_ near Brindisi, 1992; and the _[Apoxyomenos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apoxyomenos "Apoxyomenos")_ off the [Croatian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatia "Croatia") island of [Lošinj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lo%C5%A1inj "Lošinj"), 1999.

The _Victorious Youth_ was found in the summer of 1964 in the sea off [Fano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fano "Fano") on the [Adriatic coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriatic_Sea "Adriatic Sea") of Italy, snagged in the nets of an Italian fishing trawler, the _Ferri Ferruccio_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-10) Italian art dealers paid the fishermen US$5,600 for it.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-guardian-giuffrida2-1) The Getty Museum bought it from German art dealer Herman Heinz Herzer for almost US$4 million in 1977.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-guardian-giuffrida2-1) Before conservation, a thick layer of encrustation covered the statue, suggesting it has been immersed since antiquity, rather than as a result of medieval or late Venetian ships transporting the object as spoils of war or recycling it for scrap metal.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-11)

The precise location of the shipwreck, which preserved this object from being melted down like all but a tiny fraction of Greek bronzes, has not been established; it seems most likely that a [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome") ship carrying looted objects was on its way to [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy") when it sank. The statue has been roughly broken off its former base, breaking away at the ankles. The clay core inside may give further detail to where and when it was made.

## Restoration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Restoration")]

In 1972 Heinz Herzer and Volker Kinnius, the Munich gallery owner, wrote a report on the conservation project of Rudolph Stapp.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-12) Stapp, known for his specialty in ancient bronzes, was the main conservationist working on the _Victorious Youth_. Past efforts to remove encrustation from the _Bronze_ left scratches in the metal. The _Victorious Youth_ took three months to clean. First, the statue went into an artificial humidity chamber, exposing 'bronze disease'. This degradation occurs when chlorides and salts in the bronze react with moisture, producing discolored spots. If the condition is left untreated, the copper part of the bronze can easily be lost, leaving a disfigured image. The conservators neutralized the active corrosion by submerging it in a heated solution of sodium sesquicarbonate. The _Victorious Youth_ was then placed in a vacuum with the solution to penetrate interior layers without washing anything out. This process was repeated twice and was finalized with one last artificial humidity test to check for bronze disease resurfacing. An environment with a relative humidity under 35% is necessary to keep the statue from deteriorating.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-:05-2)

## Provenance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Victorious_Youth&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Provenance")]

After the bronze was retrieved in 1964 it was brought to land in Italy, where it reportedly passed through several hands on the black market.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-Kazmin,_FT_05022024-13) It emerged in 1971 under the ownership of the Artemis Consortium, an association of several international art dealers, and was then stored with a Munich art dealer, Heinz Herzer.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-14)

The [Getty Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getty_Museum "Getty Museum") is involved in a controversy regarding proper title to a number of the artwork in its collection. The Museum's previous curator of [antiquities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiquities "Antiquities"), [Marion True](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_True "Marion True"), was indicted in Italy in 2005 along with [Robert E. Hecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Hecht "Robert E. Hecht") on criminal charges relating to trafficking in stolen antiquities. The primary evidence in the case came from the 1995 raid of a [Geneva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva "Geneva"), [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland") warehouse that was found to contain stolen artifacts. Italian art dealer [Giacomo Medici](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Medici_(art_dealer) "Giacomo Medici (art dealer)") was eventually arrested in 1997; his operation was reported to be "one of the largest and most sophisticated antiquities networks in the world, responsible for illegally digging up and spiriting away thousands of top-drawer pieces and passing them on to the most elite end of the international art market".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-15) In a letter to the [J. Paul Getty Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Paul_Getty_Trust "J. Paul Getty Trust") on December 18, 2006, True stated that she was being made to "carry the burden" for practices that were known, approved, and condoned by the Getty's Board of Directors.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-16)

On November 20, 2006, the Director of the museum, [Michael Brand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Brand_(art_historian) "Michael Brand (art historian)"), announced that 26 disputed pieces were to be returned to [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"). These did not include the _Victorious Youth_, for which judicial proceedings were still pending. In an interview to the Italian national newspaper _[Corriere della Sera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corriere\_della\_Sera "Corriere della Sera")_ on December 20, 2006, the Italian Minister of Cultural Heritage declared that Italy would place the museum under a cultural embargo if all the 52 disputed pieces did not return to Italy. On August 1, 2007, an agreement was announced providing that the museum would return 40 pieces to Italy out of the 52 requested, among them the _Venus of Morgantina_, which was returned in 2010, but not the _Victorious Youth_, whose outcome depended upon the results of the criminal proceedings in Italy. On that same day the public prosecutor of Pesaro formally requested that the statue be confiscated as it was unlawfully exported out of Italy, giving rise to a dispute that came before the Constitutional Court.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-17)

Among the arguments the Getty advanced for retaining the sculpture were that, although the sculpture was retrieved by an Italian vessel, it was found in international, not Italian, waters and that it is not the work of an Italian but a Greek artist.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-Kazmin,_FT_05022024-13) However, on November 30, 2018, the [Supreme Court of Cassation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Cassation_(Italy) "Supreme Court of Cassation (Italy)") denied an appeal by the Getty Museum, affirming that Italy has a right to reclaim the _Victorious Youth_.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-18) On May 2, 2024, the [European Court of Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Court_of_Human_Rights "European Court of Human Rights") affirmed the ruling of Italy's Supreme Court of Cassation.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorious_Youth#cite_note-19)
