# The McKinley statue debate, circa 2005

[By Kevin Hoover](https://www.madriverunion.com/author/kevpod/)

on  January 06, 2018 

  

[Facebook](https://www.madriverunion.com/#facebook "Facebook")[Twitter](https://www.madriverunion.com/#twitter "Twitter")[Email](https://www.madriverunion.com/#email "Email")[Messenger](https://www.madriverunion.com/#facebook_messenger "Messenger")[Copy Link](https://www.madriverunion.com/#copy_link "Copy Link")[Message](https://www.madriverunion.com/#sms "Message")[Share](https://www.addtoany.com/share#url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.madriverunion.com%2Farticles%2Fthe-mckinley-statue-debate-circa-2005%2F&title=The%20McKinley%20statue%20debate%2C%20circa%202005)

_Note: this story was published Oct. 23, 2005 in the_ Arcata Eye._– Ed._

**Arcata Eye**

CITY HALL – Bring us the mischievous, the political, the artistic souls yearning for expression – the statue of William McKinley will remain on the Plaza, as he has for almost 100 years, one hand outstretched to receive the Groucho Marx glasses, the manifestos, the whiskey bottles and the togas.

It took two and a half hours of discussion at the City Council meeting last Wednesday to reach that conclusion, though, with vocal opinion about equally split between those who wanted to see the statue left alone or put to a City-wide vote, and those who wanted to see it moved, sold on eBay or sledgehammered to bits in the name of equality, justice and peace.  
 “From McKinley to Bush, it’s the same genocidal war,” John Garcia charged.  
 “Symbols are very, very important,” Brian Willson observed, “and this is a terrible symbol.”  
 “I don’t give a hoot if his political views were the same as mine,” countered Frances Ferguson. “He was a man of his time…. I suggest we preserve the links to our own history.”  
 As the clock rounded the bend toward 11 p.m., Councilmember Dave Meserve floated two motions, one to print an informal vote on water bills and one to put a measure on the soonest regular ballot. Both were seconded by Councilmember Paul Pitino, and both were promptly voted down by the other three councilmembers.  
 “Grant McKinley amnesty, leave him where he is and let’s move on,” Councilmember Mark Wheetley said.

![Image 2](http://madriverunion.demo.our-hometown.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/DSCN0949-640x1091.jpg)
On Oct. 9, 2005, protester Geronimo Garcia mounted McKinley to oppose the war in Iraq. KLH | Eye

**How to move a statue**

The meaning of McKinley is a regular subject of speculation at council meetings and elsewhere, and according to a staff report, has been so “for well over 30 years of which current staff is aware.” But Wednesday was the first time that discussion has made the leap onto a council agenda, gaining the needed momentum from an informal petition circulated by Sunny Brae resident Michael Schleyer.  
 City staff cautioned that the signatures collected by Schleyer aren’t legally sufficient to qualify the item for a regular election ballot, which requires the support of 10 percent of local registered voters. Incomplete addresses and post office boxes on Schleyer’s list made such verification difficult, though Deputy City Clerk Alma McCall estimated that about half of the signatures were from Arcata residents. Schleyer debated that figure, saying that by his count, almost 1,000 of the 1,451 names were from Arcata.

  
 Relocation of McKinley would require a General Plan amendment – Policy H-3g lists the statue first among Plaza features to be preserved – and, given the historic nature of the statue, an environmental impact report (EIR) as well. Community Development Director Tom Conlon noted that an EIR could cost about $30,000. The physical removal of the figure and its pedestal could cost about the same, according to the Public Works Department estimations.  
 The bronze statue was created by sculptor Haig Paitigan, survived the San Francisco earthquake of 1906 and was donated to the City of Arcata by George Zehndner on July 4, 1906.
**Bad juju**

Those who endorse moving or removing the statue of McKinley draw parallels between that administration’s foreign policies and those of the Bush administration today, arguing that McKinley represents imperialism, racism and all the other morally reprehensible aspects that have historically attended the privileged white male bastions.  
 Schleyer compared President William McKinley to Adolf Hitler, arguing that both “ordered troops to do the deed for them,” bringing about the deaths of hundreds of thousands. “It doesn’t matter to me if you kill 10 million people, two million people or 10 people,” he told the council. “You’re all in the same bag in my book.”  
 Economic Development Committeemember Shaye Harty described McKinley as “someone who makes me feel so hurt inside,” suggesting erecting a solar-powered gazebo in the statue’s place.  
 And several speakers said the racist overtones of the statue and all it stands for are so offensive that the question should not be whether it should be removed, but why it should be kept. “It is not the homeless or the weed smoke that keeps me from the Plaza,” one man accused.  
 As to the expense of moving McKinley, offers were made, variously, to defray the costs through fundraising, melting the statue down for its bronze, selling it on the internet and having a volunteer pool of laborers shoulder the dismantling responsibilities.

**Art, history**

McKinley backers didn’t have anything good to say about the president’s decisions while in office, focusing their defense instead on the significance of the near-century-old statue in the town’s history and its value as a work of art. And if the statue were to be removed based on political objections, many asked, where would such decisions stop?  
 Thomas Jefferson owned slaves, one man pointed out, and “If we don’t like Jefferson, why don’t we ban nickels in Arcata?” he joked. Another asked whether Jacoby’s Storehouse should be torn down, since it sold wares to loggers in its early years.  
 Though some of the suggestions were somewhat tongue in cheek, the idea behind them resonated with many speakers.  
 Removing the statue, Elizabeth Conner reasoned, will only remove the discussion, not the legacy. “Art should educate and create discussion,” she said.  
 “Imperialism is part of our history.” She suggested installing a plaque on the statue’s base, detailing the history of McKinley and his administration.  
 The most common argument, however, was that the decision shouldn’t be left to the five member council, but put to a vote of Arcata residents.  
 “I don’t want this City Council to decide,” former mayor Bob Ornelas emphasized. “The people should decide what to do with McKinley.”  
 To her surprise, Kathleen McCormack found herself on Ornelas’ side. “Trust me, I have never agreed with the man,” she said. “Let the entire community vote on this issue.” She also criticized some of McKinley’s critics for wearing Dockers and Nikes and supporting slave labor with their apparel choices. “I think we have an oxymoron here,” she observed.

**Vote? No.**

With an hour and a half of personal exploration out of the way, the crowd in Council Chambers dwindled to about a dozen stalwarts.  
 “I love the smell of political dialogue in the evening,” Meserve joked. He made no bones about wanting the statue gone, but he recommended circulating a two-line poll on residents’ water bills to get a sense of the City-wide opinion on the matter, avoiding – at least initially – the cost of a ballot measure. “I’d like to hear what people have to say,” he said.  
 The problems with an informal poll only multiplied as councilmembers discussed the details, though; not all residents pay their own water bills, for example, and many households have multiple occupants.  
 “I feel like this is shaping up to be some sort of hanging chad nightmare,” Wheetley laughed.  
 After initially supporting the water bill idea, Councilmember Harmony Groves shifted her support to a grassroots movement and an official petition to get the measure on a ballot.  
 And Mayor Michael Machi praised the dialogue, though he said that in a sense, an election had already been held; the long period of developing the General Plan – which ranks the McKinley statue number one for Plaza historical preservation – allowed for plenty of public input, he noted. His own priorities for the Plaza include the creation of a public bathroom, relocation of the Arcata Endeavor, funding for Arcata Police Department bike or foot patrols, removing drug users and panhandlers and maintaining a clean, safe, welcoming downtown for everyone, he said.  
 Schleyer later said that he had no plans to start circulating an official petition to remove the McKinley statue, though he said he wasn’t opposed to the idea. “For such a politically savvy town, McKinley’s a strange thing to have in the center of your town,” he said. “I wasn’t overjoyed with what happened [at the meeting], but everything happens for a reason.”

McKinley backers didn’t have anything good to say about the president’s decisions while in office, focusing their defense instead on the significance of the near-century-old statue in the town’s history and its value as a work of art. And if the statue were to be removed based on political objections, many asked, where would such decisions stop?  
 Thomas Jefferson owned slaves, one man pointed out, and “If we don’t like Jefferson, why don’t we ban nickels in Arcata?” he joked. Another asked whether Jacoby’s Storehouse should be torn down, since it sold wares to loggers in its early years.  
 Though some of the suggestions were somewhat tongue in cheek, the idea behind them resonated with many speakers.  
 Removing the statue, Elizabeth Conner reasoned, will only remove the discussion, not the legacy. “Art should educate and create discussion,” she said.  
 “Imperialism is part of our history.” She suggested installing a plaque on the statue’s base, detailing the history of McKinley and his administration.  
 The most common argument, however, was that the decision shouldn’t be left to the five member council, but put to a vote of Arcata residents.  
 “I don’t want this City Council to decide,” former mayor Bob Ornelas emphasized. “The people should decide what to do with McKinley.”  
 To her surprise, Kathleen McCormack found herself on Ornelas’ side. “Trust me, I have never agreed with the man,” she said. “Let the entire community vote on this issue.” She also criticized some of McKinley’s critics for wearing Dockers and Nikes and supporting slave labor with their apparel choices. “I think we have an oxymoron here,” she observed.

**Vote? No.**

With an hour and a half of personal exploration out of the way, the crowd in Council Chambers dwindled to about a dozen stalwarts.  
 “I love the smell of political dialogue in the evening,” Meserve joked. He made no bones about wanting the statue gone, but he recommended circulating a two-line poll on residents’ water bills to get a sense of the City-wide opinion on the matter, avoiding – at least initially – the cost of a ballot measure. “I’d like to hear what people have to say,” he said.  
 The problems with an informal poll only multiplied as councilmembers discussed the details, though; not all residents pay their own water bills, for example, and many households have multiple occupants.  
 “I feel like this is shaping up to be some sort of hanging chad nightmare,” Wheetley laughed.  
 After initially supporting the water bill idea, Councilmember Harmony Groves shifted her support to a grassroots movement and an official petition to get the measure on a ballot.  
 And Mayor Michael Machi praised the dialogue, though he said that in a sense, an election had already been held; the long period of developing the General Plan – which ranks the McKinley statue number one for Plaza historical preservation – allowed for plenty of public input, he noted. His own priorities for the Plaza include the creation of a public bathroom, relocation of the Arcata Endeavor, funding for Arcata Police Department bike or foot patrols, removing drug users and panhandlers and maintaining a clean, safe, welcoming downtown for everyone, he said.  
 Schleyer later said that he had no plans to start circulating an official petition to remove the McKinley statue, though he said he wasn’t opposed to the idea. “For such a politically savvy town, McKinley’s a strange thing to have in the center of your town,” he said. “I wasn’t overjoyed with what happened [at the meeting], but everything happens for a reason.”

GREENFIELD — Greenfield and the surrounding hilltowns are known for their picturesque roads and bike paths.

Now, the town is celebrating the freedom and joy of the cyclist, as well as Greenfield’s commitment to alternative transportation and healthy living, with a new sculpture in front of Mesa Verde that will welcome people as they walk toward Energy Park. The bronze sculpture — called “The Cyclist” — was created by Claremont, N.H.-based artist Ernest Montenegro and installed Thursday morning.

“What I ended up with was a figure of a cyclist who sort of becomes the bicycle, and that’s indicated by a gap in the front where the person sort of merges into the wheel,” Montenegro said.

The project was funded by the Massachusetts Cultural Council Adams Grant Program and the town. Greenfield solicited applications from artists last year, and a special committee selected “The Cyclist” out of seven proposals.

“What was really interesting is that Western Mass. and Greenfield are known for cycling, so it was really exciting to have a sculpture represent that,” Recreation Director Christy Moore said.

Montenegro said he had created a model of the sculpture several years ago with no intention of turning it into a commissioned piece. When he heard about Greenfield’s call to artists from a friend, he decided to submit a proposal.

GREENFIELD — Greenfield and the surrounding hilltowns are known for their picturesque roads and bike paths.

Now, the town is celebrating the freedom and joy of the cyclist, as well as Greenfield’s commitment to alternative transportation and healthy living, with a new sculpture in front of Mesa Verde that will welcome people as they walk toward Energy Park. The bronze sculpture — called “The Cyclist” — was created by Claremont, N.H.-based artist Ernest Montenegro and installed Thursday morning.

“What I ended up with was a figure of a cyclist who sort of becomes the bicycle, and that’s indicated by a gap in the front where the person sort of merges into the wheel,” Montenegro said.

The project was funded by the Massachusetts Cultural Council Adams Grant Program and the town. Greenfield solicited applications from artists last year, and a special committee selected “The Cyclist” out of seven proposals.

“What was really interesting is that Western Mass. and Greenfield are known for cycling, so it was really exciting to have a sculpture represent that,” Recreation Director Christy Moore said.

Montenegro said he had created a model of the sculpture several years ago with no intention of turning it into a commissioned piece. When he heard about Greenfield’s call to artists from a friend, he decided to submit a proposal.

## Harriet Tubman statue debate goes national

Friday is the last day to[vote for your favorite of five designs](https://billypenn.com/2023/08/04/philadelphia-harriet-tubman-statue-final-designs-vote/)for the Harriet Tubman statue planned for Philadelphia City Hall. The semifinalist artists were selected after the city reversed course on commissioning the statue from Wesley Wofford, whose[temporary version](https://billypenn.com/2022/01/16/harriet-tubman-philadelphia-statue-first-black-woman-temporary/)inspired the idea.  
  
But Wofford, a white man, was selected without any public process,[leading to an uproar](https://billypenn.com/2022/08/30/philadelphia-harriet-tubman-statue-commission-open-call-artists/)when the plan was announced. The New York Times just published[a deep dive on the controversy](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/08/30/arts/design/tubman-sculpture-philadelphia.html), asking the artists involved: Does a statue of a Black civil rights hero need to be created by someone who is Black?

![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/billypenn.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/harriettubman-statue-designs.jpg?resize=780%2C676&ssl=1)

The five semi-finalist artists’ designs for Philadelphia’s forthcoming Harriet Tubman statue. (Courtesy the artists, via the Office of Arts, Culture and Creative Economy)

## Philly teens’ relationship with social media? It’s complicated

Teenagers in Philadelphia spend a lot of time using social media apps, often frustrating parents and teachers. But while there’s no “Luddite Club” like in NYC, where teens are ditching smartphones altogether, many in Philly seem to be aware of the potential downsides — and work to self-regulate.  
  
As their last project of the summer, Billy Penn’s trio of high school interns[talked to their peers about the pros and cons of always being on their phone](https://billypenn.com/2023/08/30/philadelphia-teens-social-media-use-complicated/).

![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/billypenn.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/teen-social-media.jpg?resize=780%2C603&ssl=1)

A student in WHYY’s Pathways to Media Careers program demonstrates social media usage for the teen reporters. (Vinella Jill Vinca, Nicholas Pompey, Essie Haverkamp for Billy Penn)

## Harriet Tubman statue debate goes national

Friday is the last day to[vote for your favorite of five designs](https://billypenn.com/2023/08/04/philadelphia-harriet-tubman-statue-final-designs-vote/)for the Harriet Tubman statue planned for Philadelphia City Hall. The semifinalist artists were selected after the city reversed course on commissioning the statue from Wesley Wofford, whose[temporary version](https://billypenn.com/2022/01/16/harriet-tubman-philadelphia-statue-first-black-woman-temporary/)inspired the idea.  
  
But Wofford, a white man, was selected without any public process,[leading to an uproar](https://billypenn.com/2022/08/30/philadelphia-harriet-tubman-statue-commission-open-call-artists/)when the plan was announced. The New York Times just published[a deep dive on the controversy](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/08/30/arts/design/tubman-sculpture-philadelphia.html), asking the artists involved: Does a statue of a Black civil rights hero need to be created by someone who is Black?

![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/billypenn.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/harriettubman-statue-designs.jpg?resize=780%2C676&ssl=1)

The five semi-finalist artists’ designs for Philadelphia’s forthcoming Harriet Tubman statue. (Courtesy the artists, via the Office of Arts, Culture and Creative Economy)

## Philly teens’ relationship with social media? It’s complicated

Teenagers in Philadelphia spend a lot of time using social media apps, often frustrating parents and teachers. But while there’s no “Luddite Club” like in NYC, where teens are ditching smartphones altogether, many in Philly seem to be aware of the potential downsides — and work to self-regulate.  
  
As their last project of the summer, Billy Penn’s trio of high school interns[talked to their peers about the pros and cons of always being on their phone](https://billypenn.com/2023/08/30/philadelphia-teens-social-media-use-complicated/).

![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/billypenn.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/teen-social-media.jpg?resize=780%2C603&ssl=1)

A student in WHYY’s Pathways to Media Careers program demonstrates social media usage for the teen reporters. (Vinella Jill Vinca, Nicholas Pompey, Essie Haverkamp for Billy Penn)

# Last cyclist standing in Durango roundabout sculpture carries special meaning for artist

nd%20Videos%0A%0A%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.krqe.com%2Fnews%2Fnew-mexico%2Flast-cyclist-standing-in-durango-roundabout-sculpture-carries-special-meaning-for-artist%2F)

[DURANGO, Colo.](https://www.krqe.com/tag/durango/?ipid=dateline)(KRQE) –For the past decade, a sculpture of five cyclists has stood in the heart of Durango, Colorado. Within months, all but one of the sculptures have been destroyed.

12,000 individual steel parts and 28,000 welds, make up these five 800-pound cyclist sculptures, that were installed on Florida Road near Chapman Hill in Durango in 2012. “Not many problems leading up to this point, but on March 8th, we had one driver crash into the center roundabout, destroying three of the five cyclist statues,” said Sgt. Michael Kelly, Durango Police Department.

Roughly two months later, “We had another individual lose control and at the round about taking out one more of the statues,” said Kelly.

Joshua Wiener, the artist behind the sculpture is now tasked with the repairs. But it’s one piece of the surviving sculpture, that he said is warming his heart through the process. Modeled after his own brother, the lone cyclist still stands today, with an orange vest and helmet.

His brother Adam, an avid cyclist, inspired Joshua to fall in love with the hobby too. Before Adam lost his life to ALS, Joshua shared the piece with him. “I think it was sweet for him. I think he was honored. But he didn’t make a big deal of it. I think he was pretty humble. It was more me telling my big brother I love him,” said Wiener.

Durango Police said the first crash was caused by an impaired driver, who was arrested. The driver in the second crash was an elderly man, who was cited for careless driving. The artist hopes to have the sculptures repaired by the end of June.

# Last cyclist standing in Durango roundabout sculpture carries special meaning for artist

nd%20Videos%0A%0A%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.krqe.com%2Fnews%2Fnew-mexico%2Flast-cyclist-standing-in-durango-roundabout-sculpture-carries-special-meaning-for-artist%2F)

[DURANGO, Colo.](https://www.krqe.com/tag/durango/?ipid=dateline)(KRQE) –For the past decade, a sculpture of five cyclists has stood in the heart of Durango, Colorado. Within months, all but one of the sculptures have been destroyed.

12,000 individual steel parts and 28,000 welds, make up these five 800-pound cyclist sculptures, that were installed on Florida Road near Chapman Hill in Durango in 2012. “Not many problems leading up to this point, but on March 8th, we had one driver crash into the center roundabout, destroying three of the five cyclist statues,” said Sgt. Michael Kelly, Durango Police Department.

Roughly two months later, “We had another individual lose control and at the round about taking out one more of the statues,” said Kelly.

Joshua Wiener, the artist behind the sculpture is now tasked with the repairs. But it’s one piece of the surviving sculpture, that he said is warming his heart through the process. Modeled after his own brother, the lone cyclist still stands today, with an orange vest and helmet.

His brother Adam, an avid cyclist, inspired Joshua to fall in love with the hobby too. Before Adam lost his life to ALS, Joshua shared the piece with him. “I think it was sweet for him. I think he was honored. But he didn’t make a big deal of it. I think he was pretty humble. It was more me telling my big brother I love him,” said Wiener.

Durango Police said the first crash was caused by an impaired driver, who was arrested. The driver in the second crash was an elderly man, who was cited for careless driving. The artist hopes to have the sculptures repaired by the end of June.

# City working with artist and insurance to repair "Endurance" Sculptures

 City of Durango News Flash  Posted on March 11, 2026 

**Durango, CO:**The City of Durango is in contact with the artist Joshua Wiener and its insurance company to work toward restoring the “Endurance” roundabout sculptures on Florida Road near Chapman Hill following the recent crash.

“Our insurance will cover repairs, and the artist is in the loop to try and repair the sculptures,” Economic Opportunity Manager Tommy Crosby said.

The city’s Safety and Risk Administrator, Sara Easley, said the next steps are to remove the damaged parts of the sculpture, work with the artist on a cost estimate for repairs, and submit an insurance claim.

“At this point, we will be looking to remove the damaged pieces in the next couple of weeks, but the restoration will probably take some time,” Easley said.

The public art piece was placed at the roundabout in 2012 and was constructed using 12,000 individual steel parts and 28,000 welds.

The five 800-pound cyclist sculptures were created to commemorate the USA Pro Cycling Challenge. A chair member for the event reached out to the city and said that it was a requirement of the pro challenge to leave a permanent commemorative art piece, and that a $25,000 contribution from the Bank of Colorado was secured to fund the sculpture.

The damage was caused by an impaired driver who crashed into the art piece on March 8. The Durango Police Department released a social media post on the night of the crash, reminding residents of the dangers of driving under the influence of drugs and alcohol.

The post said, “Today, those bicyclists were artwork. Next time, they could be someone’s loved one.”

A proud day for Cahersiveen and a wonderful tribute ahead of today’s official unveiling.

The **Monuments** are five [classic cycle races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_cycle_races "Classic cycle races") generally considered to be the oldest, hardest, longest and most prestigious one-day events in men's [road cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_bicycle_racing "Road bicycle racing"), with distances between 240 and 300 kilometres (150 and 190 mi).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-3)As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cycling_monument&action=edit), all monuments except [Giro di Lombardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_di_Lombardia "Giro di Lombardia") hold women's races as part of the [UCI Women's World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCI_Women's_World_Tour "UCI Women's World Tour").

Each has a long history and varied characteristics. They are the one-day races in which most points can be earned in the [UCI World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCI_World_Tour "UCI World Tour") and the only 3rd categorized UCI races, behind only [Grand Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour_(cycling) "Grand Tour (cycling)") races: [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_France "Tour de France") (1st category) and [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_d'Italia "Giro d'Italia") and [Vuelta a España](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vuelta_a_Espa%C3%B1a "Vuelta a España") (both 2nd category).

With 19 wins, [Eddy Merckx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx "Eddy Merckx") is by far the most successful monument rider. He won three monuments in a single season in 1969, 1971, 1972 and 1975. [Tadej Pogačar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadej_Poga%C4%8Dar "Tadej Pogačar") is the only other rider to achieve the feat, doing so in 2025 and 2026.

Held in March, it is the first major classic of the season.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-uci-msr-4) First held in 1907, it is by far the longest one-day race on the UCI calendar at nearly 300 km (190 mi). Due to its flat profile, it is considered a [sprinter's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_sprinter "Cycling sprinter") classic, but the famous finishing climbs of [the Cipressa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cipressa "Cipressa") and [the Poggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poggio_di_San_Remo "Poggio di San Remo") give other types of cyclists a chance to win.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-uci-msr-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-msr-5) It is often described as "the easiest Monument to finish, but the hardest to win".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-msr-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-6)
*   [![Image 11: Belgium](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Flag_of_Belgium_%28civil%29.svg/40px-Flag_of_Belgium_%28civil%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium")[Tour of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_of_Flanders_(men's_race) "Tour of Flanders (men's race)"): the _Ronde van Vlaanderen_ in Dutch, or simply _De Ronde_ ("the Tour"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-bbc-rvv-7) is raced on the first Sunday in April.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-rvv-8) First held in 1913,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-bbc-rvv-7) the race typically covers more than 270 km (170 mi) in the [Flemish Ardennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_Ardennes "Flemish Ardennes") and is known for its short, steep hills and cobbled sections.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-rvv-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-rouleur-rvv-9) The course shifts from year to year, with the start switching between [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp") and [Bruges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruges "Bruges") in recent years.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-rvv-8) A key point is the [Oude Kwaremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oude_Kwaremont "Oude Kwaremont"), the longest climb of the race at 2.2 km (1.4 mi) long with a max gradient of 11%.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-rouleur-rvv-9)
*   [![Image 12: France](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/c/c3/Flag_of_France.svg/40px-Flag_of_France.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France")[Paris–Roubaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Roubaix "Paris–Roubaix"): also called "the Queen of the Classics" or "the Hell of the North", it is raced in April one week after the Tour of Flanders and is the final [cobbled classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobbled_classics "Cobbled classics"). First organized in 1896, the race started in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") up to 1967, before switching to the current start in [Compiègne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compi%C3%A8gne "Compiègne"), and is approximately 260 km.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-pr-10) The race is known for its long sections of _pavé_ (cobblestone roads), with 30 cobbled sectors totaling over 50 km (31 mi), including the difficult [Trouée d'Arenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trou%C3%A9e_d'Arenberg "Trouée d'Arenberg") before finishing in the [Roubaix Velodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roubaix_Velodrome "Roubaix Velodrome"). It is considered the toughest monument,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-guide-11) as well as "arguably the most recognizable" one-day race on the cycling calendar.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-pr-10)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-12)
*   [![Image 13: Belgium](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Flag_of_Belgium_%28civil%29.svg/40px-Flag_of_Belgium_%28civil%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium")[Liège–Bastogne–Liège](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li%C3%A8ge%E2%80%93Bastogne%E2%80%93Li%C3%A8ge "Liège–Bastogne–Liège"): known as _La Doyenne_ ("the old lady"[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-13) or "the oldest"[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-14)), it is the final [Ardennes classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardennes_classics "Ardennes classics"), usually held in late April as the last of the spring one-day races. First organized in 1892, it is the oldest monument.[[notes 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-lbl-16) The 250 km (160 mi) course is considered a "war of attrition" due to its difficult hilly terrain, favouring [climbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climbing_specialist "Climbing specialist") or even [Grand Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour_(cycling) "Grand Tour (cycling)") specialists.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-lbl-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-17)
*   [![Image 14: Italy](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/03/Flag_of_Italy.svg/40px-Flag_of_Italy.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")[Giro di Lombardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_di_Lombardia "Giro di Lombardia"): also called the _classica delle foglie morte_ ("race of the falling leaves"), it is the final monument of the season, usually held in October.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-guide-11) First held in 1905, it was initially organized as _Milano–Milano_. The course switches between starting and finishing in [Como](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Como "Como") and [Bergamo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergamo "Bergamo"), and is known for its hilly terrain around [Lake Como](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Como "Lake Como"). Similar to Liège–Bastogne–Liège, it is considered a climber's classic, ascending difficult hills such as [Madonna del Ghisallo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna_del_Ghisallo "Madonna del Ghisallo").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-18)

## Origin

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cycling_monument&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origin")]

The expression "cycling monument" has been used since the early days of cycle racing. In 1904, [Henri Desgrange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Desgrange "Henri Desgrange") wrote in [L'Auto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Auto "L'Auto") that "The "Tour de France" is over and its second edition will, I fear, have also been the last. [...] And yet, it seemed to us and it still seems to us that we had built with this great event the most lasting and most imposing monument to the sport of cycling".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-19)

In 1949, French sports journalist [Albert Baker d'Isy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Baker_d'Isy "Albert Baker d'Isy") wrote about the 47th edition of the [Paris–Roubaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Paris%E2%80%93Roubaix "1949 Paris–Roubaix") race, titling his article in the French newspaper [Ce soir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ce_soir "Ce soir") "_Paris–Roubaix: "monument" du cyclisme"._ The term was used again by journalist [Jacques Goddet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Goddet "Jacques Goddet") in 1950, writing about Fausto Coppi's victory at [Paris–Roubaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Paris%E2%80%93Roubaix "1949 Paris–Roubaix") – "Monument of international cycling, Paris-Roubaix crushed the riders with its legend as well as its diabolical difficulties".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:0-20)

When the [Super Prestige Pernod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Prestige_Pernod "Super Prestige Pernod") had to be abandoned at the end of 1987, [Hein Verbruggen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hein_Verbruggen "Hein Verbruggen") (president of the [FICP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FICP "FICP")) went on to create a new competition (which became the [UCI Road World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCI_Road_World_Cup "UCI Road World Cup")), where five races were given a fixed position under the name 'cycling monument', and these were the five races still known as monuments.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-21)

The term began being used more by the [Union Cycliste Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Cycliste_Internationale "Union Cycliste Internationale") (UCI) and cycling media at the end of the 20th century,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:1-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:5-23) with the term designating the five most prestigious [classic cycle races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_cycle_races "Classic cycle races"), namely [Milan–San Remo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan%E2%80%93San_Remo "Milan–San Remo"), [Tour of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_of_Flanders_(men's_race) "Tour of Flanders (men's race)"), Paris–Roubaix, [Liège–Bastogne–Liège](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li%C3%A8ge%E2%80%93Bastogne%E2%80%93Li%C3%A8ge "Liège–Bastogne–Liège") and [Giro di Lombardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_di_Lombardia "Giro di Lombardia").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:1-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:5-23)

Since 2010, the races are considered by the [Union Cycliste Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Cycliste_Internationale "Union Cycliste Internationale") to be more prestigious than other one-day races that are raced by the professional peloton, with only the [Grand Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour_(cycling) "Grand Tour (cycling)") stage races gaining more ranking points for the winner.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:0-20)

In 2017, _[L'Équipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'%C3%89quipe "L'Équipe")_ wrote that the five monuments were "the oldest one-day races, the most famous, the most unique" and that they had "prestigious entry fields" of champion riders.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:0-20)

## Future monuments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cycling_monument&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Future monuments")]

Media and riders have discussed whether other classic cycling races meet the criteria of a cycling monument. By the 2020s, [Strade Bianche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strade_Bianche "Strade Bianche") – an Italian one-day race first held in 2007, defined by its use of white gravel roads – was considered to be the most likely candidate,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:2-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:3-26) with [_Cycling News_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclingnews.com "Cyclingnews.com") stating in 2025 that "there is no longer any debate that Strade Bianche is cycling's sixth Monument".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-27) However, others have criticised that Strade Bianche does not have the length or longevity to be titled a monument,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-28) and rider [Philippe Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_Gilbert "Philippe Gilbert") noted that [Clásica de San Sebastián](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cl%C3%A1sica_de_San_Sebasti%C3%A1n "Clásica de San Sebastián") and [Amstel Gold Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amstel_Gold_Race_(men's_race) "Amstel Gold Race (men's race)") were more important historically.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-29)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:1-22)

In the women's tour, media have suggested that [Trofeo Alfredo Binda-Comune di Cittiglio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trofeo_Alfredo_Binda-Comune_di_Cittiglio "Trofeo Alfredo Binda-Comune di Cittiglio") (the oldest one-day race on the women's calendar) and [Strade Bianche Donne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strade_Bianche_Donne "Strade Bianche Donne") may be worthy of the "monument" moniker.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:2-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:3-26)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:4-30)

The **Monuments** are five [classic cycle races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_cycle_races "Classic cycle races") generally considered to be the oldest, hardest, longest and most prestigious one-day events in men's [road cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_bicycle_racing "Road bicycle racing"), with distances between 240 and 300 kilometres (150 and 190 mi).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-3)As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cycling_monument&action=edit), all monuments except [Giro di Lombardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_di_Lombardia "Giro di Lombardia") hold women's races as part of the [UCI Women's World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCI_Women's_World_Tour "UCI Women's World Tour").

Each has a long history and varied characteristics. They are the one-day races in which most points can be earned in the [UCI World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCI_World_Tour "UCI World Tour") and the only 3rd categorized UCI races, behind only [Grand Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour_(cycling) "Grand Tour (cycling)") races: [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_France "Tour de France") (1st category) and [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_d'Italia "Giro d'Italia") and [Vuelta a España](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vuelta_a_Espa%C3%B1a "Vuelta a España") (both 2nd category).

With 19 wins, [Eddy Merckx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx "Eddy Merckx") is by far the most successful monument rider. He won three monuments in a single season in 1969, 1971, 1972 and 1975. [Tadej Pogačar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadej_Poga%C4%8Dar "Tadej Pogačar") is the only other rider to achieve the feat, doing so in 2025 and 2026.

Held in March, it is the first major classic of the season.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-uci-msr-4) First held in 1907, it is by far the longest one-day race on the UCI calendar at nearly 300 km (190 mi). *   [![Image 11: Belgium](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Flag_of_Belgium_%28civil%29.svg/40px-Flag_of_Belgium_%28civil%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium")[Tour of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_of_Flanders_(men's_race) "Tour of Flanders (men's race)"): the _Ronde van Vlaanderen_ in Dutch, or simply _De Ronde_ ("the Tour"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-bbc-rvv-7) is raced on the first Sunday in April.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-rvv-8) First held in 1913,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-bbc-rvv-7) the race typically covers more than 270 km (170 mi) in the [Flemish Ardennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_Ardennes "Flemish Ardennes") and is known for its short, steep hills and cobbled sections.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-rvv-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-rouleur-rvv-9) The course shifts from year to year, with the start switching between [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp") and [Bruges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruges "Bruges") in recent years.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-rvv-8) A key point is the [Oude Kwaremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oude_Kwaremont "Oude Kwaremont"), the longest climb of the race at 2.2 km (1.4 mi) long with a max gradient of 11%.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-rouleur-rvv-9)
*   [![Image 12: France](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/c/c3/Flag_of_France.svg/40px-Flag_of_France.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France")[Paris–Roubaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Roubaix "Paris–Roubaix"): also called "the Queen of the Classics" or "the Hell of the North", it is raced in April one week after the Tour of Flanders and is the final [cobbled classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobbled_classics "Cobbled classics"). First organized in 1896, the race started in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") up to 1967, before switching to the current start in [Compiègne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compi%C3%A8gne "Compiègne"), and is approximately 260 km.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-pr-10) The race is known for its long sections of _pavé_ (cobblestone roads), with 30 cobbled sectors totaling over 50 km (31 mi), including the difficult [Trouée d'Arenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trou%C3%A9e_d'Arenberg "Trouée d'Arenberg") before finishing in the [Roubaix Velodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roubaix_Velodrome "Roubaix Velodrome"). It is considered the toughest monument,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-guide-11) as well as "arguably the most recognizable" one-day race on the cycling calendar.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-pr-10)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-12)
*   [![Image 13: Belgium](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Flag_of_Belgium_%28civil%29.svg/40px-Flag_of_Belgium_%28civil%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium")[Liège–Bastogne–Liège](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li%C3%A8ge%E2%80%93Bastogne%E2%80%93Li%C3%A8ge "Liège–Bastogne–Liège"): known as _La Doyenne_ ("the old lady"[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-13) or "the oldest"[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-14)), it is the final [Ardennes classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardennes_classics "Ardennes classics"), usually held in late April as the last of the spring one-day races. First organized in 1892, it is the oldest monument.[[notes 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-lbl-16) The 250 km (160 mi) course is considered a "war of attrition" due to its difficult hilly terrain, favouring [climbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climbing_specialist "Climbing specialist") or even [Grand Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour_(cycling) "Grand Tour (cycling)") specialists.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-lbl-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-17)
*   [![Image 14: Italy](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/03/Flag_of_Italy.svg/40px-Flag_of_Italy.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")[Giro di Lombardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_di_Lombardia "Giro di Lombardia"): also called the _classica delle foglie morte_ ("race of the falling leaves"), it is the final monument of the season, usually held in October.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-cn-guide-11) First held in 1905, it was initially organized as _Milano–Milano_. The course switches between starting and finishing in [Como](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Como "Como") and [Bergamo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergamo "Bergamo"), and is known for its hilly terrain around [Lake Como](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Como "Lake Como"). Similar to Liège–Bastogne–Liège, it is considered a climber's classic, ascending difficult hills such as [Madonna del Ghisallo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna_del_Ghisallo "Madonna del Ghisallo").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-18)

## Origin

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cycling_monument&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origin")]

The expression "cycling monument" has been used since the early days of cycle racing. In 1904, [Henri Desgrange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Desgrange "Henri Desgrange") wrote in [L'Auto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Auto "L'Auto") that "The "Tour de France" is over and its second edition will, I fear, have also been the last. [...] And yet, it seemed to us and it still seems to us that we had built with this great event the most lasting and most imposing monument to the sport of cycling".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-19)

In 1949, French sports journalist [Albert Baker d'Isy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Baker_d'Isy "Albert Baker d'Isy") wrote about the 47th edition of the [Paris–Roubaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Paris%E2%80%93Roubaix "1949 Paris–Roubaix") race, titling his article in the French newspaper [Ce soir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ce_soir "Ce soir") "_Paris–Roubaix: "monument" du cyclisme"._ The term was used again by journalist [Jacques Goddet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Goddet "Jacques Goddet") in 1950, writing about Fausto Coppi's victory at [Paris–Roubaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Paris%E2%80%93Roubaix "1949 Paris–Roubaix") – "Monument of international cycling, Paris-Roubaix crushed the riders with its legend as well as its diabolical difficulties".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:0-20)

When the [Super Prestige Pernod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Prestige_Pernod "Super Prestige Pernod") had to be abandoned at the end of 1987, [Hein Verbruggen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hein_Verbruggen "Hein Verbruggen") (president of the [FICP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FICP "FICP")) went on to create a new competition (which became the [UCI Road World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCI_Road_World_Cup "UCI Road World Cup")), where five races were given a fixed position under the name 'cycling monument', and these were the five races still known as monuments.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-21)

The term began being used more by the [Union Cycliste Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Cycliste_Internationale "Union Cycliste Internationale") (UCI) and cycling media at the end of the 20th century,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:1-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:5-23) with the term designating the five most prestigious [classic cycle races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_cycle_races "Classic cycle races"), namely [Milan–San Remo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan%E2%80%93San_Remo "Milan–San Remo"), [Tour of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_of_Flanders_(men's_race) "Tour of Flanders (men's race)"), Paris–Roubaix, [Liège–Bastogne–Liège](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li%C3%A8ge%E2%80%93Bastogne%E2%80%93Li%C3%A8ge "Liège–Bastogne–Liège") and [Giro di Lombardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_di_Lombardia "Giro di Lombardia").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:1-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:5-23)

Since 2010, the races are considered by the [Union Cycliste Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Cycliste_Internationale "Union Cycliste Internationale") to be more prestigious than other one-day races that are raced by the professional peloton, with only the [Grand Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour_(cycling) "Grand Tour (cycling)") stage races gaining more ranking points for the winner.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:0-20)

In 2017, _[L'Équipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'%C3%89quipe "L'Équipe")_ wrote that the five monuments were "the oldest one-day races, the most famous, the most unique" and that they had "prestigious entry fields" of champion riders.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:0-20)

## Future monuments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cycling_monument&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Future monuments")]

Media and riders have discussed whether other classic cycling races meet the criteria of a cycling monument. By the 2020s, [Strade Bianche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strade_Bianche "Strade Bianche") – an Italian one-day race first held in 2007, defined by its use of white gravel roads – was considered to be the most likely candidate,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:2-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:3-26) with [_Cycling News_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclingnews.com "Cyclingnews.com") stating in 2025 that "there is no longer any debate that Strade Bianche is cycling's sixth Monument".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-27) However, others have criticised that Strade Bianche does not have the length or longevity to be titled a monument,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-28) and rider [Philippe Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_Gilbert "Philippe Gilbert") noted that [Clásica de San Sebastián](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cl%C3%A1sica_de_San_Sebasti%C3%A1n "Clásica de San Sebastián") and [Amstel Gold Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amstel_Gold_Race_(men's_race) "Amstel Gold Race (men's race)") were more important historically.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-29)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:1-22)

In the women's tour, media have suggested that [Trofeo Alfredo Binda-Comune di Cittiglio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trofeo_Alfredo_Binda-Comune_di_Cittiglio "Trofeo Alfredo Binda-Comune di Cittiglio") (the oldest one-day race on the women's calendar) and [Strade Bianche Donne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strade_Bianche_Donne "Strade Bianche Donne") may be worthy of the "monument" moniker.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:2-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:3-26)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument#cite_note-:4-30)

# New statue is salute to ‘The Cyclist’

![Image 4](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/bb83e857792a46fb33d89fd333b66f16d77dca43f24444f66ee892add1a4a9ae?s=96&d=mm&r=g)by [Aviva Luttrell](https://recorder.com/author/aviva-luttrell/) Recorder Staff June 1, 2017

GREENFIELD — Greenfield and the surrounding hilltowns are known for their picturesque roads and bike paths.

Now, the town is celebrating the freedom and joy of the cyclist, as well as Greenfield’s commitment to alternative transportation and healthy living, with a new sculpture in front of Mesa Verde that will welcome people as they walk toward Energy Park. The bronze sculpture — called “The Cyclist” — was created by Claremont, N.H.-based artist Ernest Montenegro and installed Thursday morning.

“What I ended up with was a figure of a cyclist who sort of becomes the bicycle, and that’s indicated by a gap in the front where the person sort of merges into the wheel,” Montenegro said.

The project was funded by the Massachusetts Cultural Council Adams Grant Program and the town. Greenfield solicited applications from artists last year, and a special committee selected “The Cyclist” out of seven proposals.

“What was really interesting is that Western Mass. and Greenfield are known for cycling, so it was really exciting to have a sculpture represent that,” Recreation Director Christy Moore said.

Montenegro said he had created a model of the sculpture several years ago with no intention of turning it into a commissioned piece. When he heard about Greenfield’s call to artists from a friend, he decided to submit a proposal.

“Each one is different,” he said. “In each instance I tried to not do what’s called helicopter something in and just drop it on the site if it had nothing to do with the community or the area. I try to be sensitive about what the community is about, up to a point. There’s a limit to that, you have to balance the privileges of art with what people expect.”

The sculpture was cast by Campbell Plaster and Iron in West Rutland, Vt. and Negus & Taylor of Greenfield donated a 3,600-pound piece of granite for the base.

Moore said the town plans to hold a ribbon cutting ceremony sometime in July.

“It’s inviting, it draws people down to the sculpture and we hope that they will the make their way down to the Energy Park,” she said.

# New statue is salute to ‘The Cyclist’

GREENFIELD — Greenfield and the surrounding hilltowns are known for their picturesque roads and bike paths.

Now, the town is celebrating the freedom and joy of the cyclist, as well as Greenfield’s commitment to alternative transportation and healthy living, with a new sculpture in front of Mesa Verde that will welcome people as they walk toward Energy Park. The bronze sculpture — called “The Cyclist” — was created by Claremont, N.H.-based artist Ernest Montenegro and installed Thursday morning.

“What I ended up with was a figure of a cyclist who sort of becomes the bicycle, and that’s indicated by a gap in the front where the person sort of merges into the wheel,” Montenegro said.

The project was funded by the Massachusetts Cultural Council Adams Grant Program and the town. Greenfield solicited applications from artists last year, and a special committee selected “The Cyclist” out of seven proposals.

“What was really interesting is that Western Mass. and Greenfield are known for cycling, so it was really exciting to have a sculpture represent that,” Recreation Director Christy Moore said.

Montenegro said he had created a model of the sculpture several years ago with no intention of turning it into a commissioned piece. When he heard about Greenfield’s call to artists from a friend, he decided to submit a proposal.

The sculpture was cast by Campbell Plaster and Iron in West Rutland, Vt. and Negus & Taylor of Greenfield donated a 3,600-pound piece of granite for the base.

Moore said the town plans to hold a ribbon cutting ceremony sometime in July.

“It’s inviting, it draws people down to the sculpture and we hope that they will the make their way down to the Energy Park,” she said.

# Last cyclist standing in Durango roundabout sculpture carries special meaning for artist

nd%20Videos%0A%0A%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.krqe.com%2Fnews%2Fnew-mexico%2Flast-cyclist-standing-in-durango-roundabout-sculpture-carries-special-meaning-for-artist%2F)

[DURANGO, Colo.](https://www.krqe.com/tag/durango/?ipid=dateline)(KRQE) –For the past decade, a sculpture of five cyclists has stood in the heart of Durango, Colorado. Within months, all but one of the sculptures have been destroyed.

12,000 individual steel parts and 28,000 welds, make up these five 800-pound cyclist sculptures, that were installed on Florida Road near Chapman Hill in Durango in 2012. “Not many problems leading up to this point, but on March 8th, we had one driver crash into the center roundabout, destroying three of the five cyclist statues,” said Sgt. Michael Kelly, Durango Police Department.

Roughly two months later, “We had another individual lose control and at the round about taking out one more of the statues,” said Kelly.

Joshua Wiener, the artist behind the sculpture is now tasked with the repairs. But it’s one piece of the surviving sculpture, that he said is warming his heart through the process. Modeled after his own brother, the lone cyclist still stands today, with an orange vest and helmet.

Video 4

Video 5

His brother Adam, an avid cyclist, inspired Joshua to fall in love with the hobby too. Before Adam lost his life to ALS, Joshua shared the piece with him. “I think it was sweet for him. I think he was honored. But he didn’t make a big deal of it. I think he was pretty humble. It was more me telling my big brother I love him,” said Wiener.

Durango Police said the first crash was caused by an impaired driver, who was arrested. The driver in the second crash was an elderly man, who was cited for careless driving. The artist hopes to have the sculptures repaired by the end of June.

# Last cyclist standing in Durango roundabout sculpture carries special meaning for artist

nd%20Videos%0A%0A%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.krqe.com%2Fnews%2Fnew-mexico%2Flast-cyclist-standing-in-durango-roundabout-sculpture-carries-special-meaning-for-artist%2F)

[DURANGO, Colo.](https://www.krqe.com/tag/durango/?ipid=dateline)(KRQE) –For the past decade, a sculpture of five cyclists has stood in the heart of Durango, Colorado. Within months, all but one of the sculptures have been destroyed.

12,000 individual steel parts and 28,000 welds, make up these five 800-pound cyclist sculptures, that were installed on Florida Road near Chapman Hill in Durango in 2012. “Not many problems leading up to this point, but on March 8th, we had one driver crash into the center roundabout, destroying three of the five cyclist statues,” said Sgt. Michael Kelly, Durango Police Department.

Roughly two months later, “We had another individual lose control and at the round about taking out one more of the statues,” said Kelly.

Joshua Wiener, the artist behind the sculpture is now tasked with the repairs. But it’s one piece of the surviving sculpture, that he said is warming his heart through the process. Modeled after his own brother, the lone cyclist still stands today, with an orange vest and helmet.

Video 4

Video 5

His brother Adam, an avid cyclist, inspired Joshua to fall in love with the hobby too. Before Adam lost his life to ALS, Joshua shared the piece with him. “I think it was sweet for him. I think he was honored. But he didn’t make a big deal of it. I think he was pretty humble. It was more me telling my big brother I love him,” said Wiener.

Durango Police said the first crash was caused by an impaired driver, who was arrested. The driver in the second crash was an elderly man, who was cited for careless driving. The artist hopes to have the sculptures repaired by the end of June.

[![Image 5: He thought he'd stumbled upon a tragedy. Instead, the arm jutting out from the seabed was bronze, dating back 2,400 years, and belonged to one of ancient Greece's most breathtaking masterpieces. August 16, 1972. The coast of Riace Marina, Calabria, southern Italy. Stefano Mariottini, a chemistry enthusiast and amateur diver from Rome, was exploring the shallow waters about 200 meters from shore. The water was crystal clear, roughly 8 meters deep. Then, he spotted an arm protruding from the sand. At first, his thoughts were dire: a drowning victim. He swam closer for a better look. The arm was bronze. Mariottini gently brushed away more sand. Instead of a body, a statue emerged—a life-sized bronze warrior, remarkably preserved, lying on the seabed as if waiting for centuries. Which, as it turned out, it had. Mariottini continued his search and discovered a second statue nearby, equally well-preserved. He notified local authorities about his find. Within days, archaeologists arrived and meticulously retrieved both statues from the seafloor. What they uncovered stunned the archaeological community. These were Greek bronze statues from the 5th century BC—the golden era of Classical Greek sculpture, around 460-450 BC. And they were almost intact. This is extraordinarily rare. Ancient bronze statues rarely survive. Bronze was valuable and often melted down throughout history—by Romans for weapons, by medieval Europeans repurposing materials, by anyone in need of bronze. Most knowledge of Greek bronze sculpture comes from Roman marble replicas made centuries later. Original Greek bronze pieces are extremely rare. But these two warriors lay hidden beneath layers of sand on the Mediterranean seabed for over 2,000 years. The sand acted as a protective layer, preventing corrosion and preserving details otherwise lost. Upon close examination, archaeologists found stunning details: Individual muscles crafted with anatomical precision. Visible veins under the skin. Each year, crowds of spectators pack arenas and stadiums to watch their favorite athletes in action. Fans idolize them, young athletes want to be them and corporate sponsors want to work with them.

However, like millions of Americans, athletes grapple with drug and alcohol addictions. Rarely a day passes without news of a player entering rehab, failing a drug test, partying lavishly or [overdosing on a substance](https://www.drugrehab.com/guides/overdose/).

Professional sports foster [substance abuse](https://www.drugrehab.com/addiction/). Many athletes are highly paid and can easily access drugs through their social circles. This has led to a substance abuse epidemic that has shattered the lives of countless athletes.

![Image 9: Football teams on the starting line](https://www.drugrehab.com/wp-content/themes/dr/images/athletes/WhyAthletesTurn-Image.jpg)
## Why athletes turn to drugs

Athletes turn to drugs for various reasons. Some do so to enhance their performance or remedy an injury. Others pick up an addiction after entering professional sports.

*   Enhanced Performance
*   Injuries
*   Depression
*   Accessibility
*   Personal History

### Enhanced Performance

Athletes are caught in high-pressure situations during contests. However, these moments pale in comparison to the pressures that come with success.

In response, countless competitors have turned to performance-enhancing drugs, or PEDs, to obtain a competitive edge. These substances increase physical attributes but present numerous health risks. Various PEDs are banned from usage in all major sports in the United States.

In 2009, Alex Rodriguez, who admitted to using steroids, told ESPN, “When I arrived in Texas in 2001, I felt an enormous amount of pressure. I felt like I had all the weight of the world on top of me and I needed to perform, and perform at a high level, every day.”

### Injuries

Many injured athletes use drugs to accelerate their recovery. This has led to substance abuse.

Athletes in speed and power sports often use nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as their remedy. According to a 2008 study published in Sports Medicine, elite athletes use medications to treat asthma more frequently than the general population does. These drugs are most common in endurance sports like cycling and swimming.

However, using medications can lead to addiction. Football player Erik Ainge took prescription painkillers for a broken finger in college, which gave way to an addiction that continued for years.

Many have turned to marijuana to alleviate chronic pain. The drug is legal in several states and players have said it is a safer option than prescription pills. NFL player Eugene Monroe in 2016 called cannabis a healthier alternative to opioids.

However, many leagues prohibit its use. Marijuana use in professional sports can lead to suspensions and lifetime bans.

### Depression

[Depression](https://www.drugrehab.com/co-occurring-disorder/depression/) is a mental health disorder that affects millions of Americans each year, including athletes.

Frédéric Weis, a professional basketball player, fell into a depression after his son was diagnosed with autism in 2002. In response, he turned to alcohol. In 2008, he survived a suicide attempt that involved [sleeping pills](https://www.drugrehab.com/addiction/are-sleeping-pills-safe/).

In 2011, boxing legend Oscar De La Hoya told Univision how depression led to his addictions to cocaine and alcohol. He had thoughts of suicide before entering a rehab facility earlier that year.

### Accessibility

Athletes obtain addictive substances from medical and nonmedical sources.

For example, Michael Bell, a former professional wrestler, received hundreds of painkillers from fellow wrestlers, which triggered an addiction. He later died of unknown causes at a rehab center. Bell’s brother Chris chronicled Michael’s story in “Prescription Thugs,” a documentary about America’s legal drug abuse problem.

Derek Boogaard, an ice hockey player who died of an accidental overdose of oxycodone and alcohol, received more than 100 prescriptions for pills during his final three years of life. Most pills were administered by team physicians.

“To see him have all that access to those doctors and all those prescriptions, that is mind boggling,” Dr. Louis Baxter Sr., executive medical director of the Professional Assistance Program of New Jersey and immediate past president of the American Society of Addiction Medicine, told The New York Times. “He had such easy access to prescription medicines.”

Former NFL quarterback Jim McMahon said he received hundreds of injections and pills from team medical professionals, including Percocet, Toradol and amphetamines, per The Washington Post.

In recent years, professional leagues have been publicly scrutinized for contributing to this epidemic. In 2014, DEA agents conducted a random inspection on NFL teams in an ongoing investigation into [prescription drug abuse](https://www.drugrehab.com/addiction/prescription-drugs/). The DEA made no arrests and did not report any irregularities.

### Personal History

Traumatic events early in life could lead to [drug addiction](https://www.drugrehab.com/addiction/drugs/).

As a child, former boxer Johnny Tapia witnessed his mother’s murder. The event triggered a lifelong alcohol and [cocaine addiction](https://www.drugrehab.com/addiction/drugs/cocaine/), suicide attempts and multiple incarcerations. He was declared dead four different times due to drug overdoses. In 2012, he died of heart failure.

Professional golfer John Daly grew up around alcohol, which led to his own problems with the substance. His father in 2006 told USA Today, “I taught him to drink. My mother let me drink at home. I let my kids drink at home. It’s what we did back then.”

According to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, the arts, entertainment and recreation industry ranked second in past-month illicit drug use and third in past-year substance use disorder rates from 2008 to 2012. The industry includes professional athletes.

### Len Bias

Len Bias was a star basketball player at the University of Maryland, earning the ACC Athlete of the Year and ACC Player of the Year awards in 1986. He was selected by the Boston Celtics with the second pick in the 1986 NBA draft, expected to join a team that included Larry Bird, Kevin McHale and Robert Parrish.

At 22, Bias died of cardiac arrhythmia caused by a [cocaine overdose](https://www.drugrehab.com/addiction/drugs/cocaine/overdose/) two days after he was drafted. It was one of the youngest drug-related deaths in professional sports.

“During my years as an ACC coach, the two most dominant players we’ve faced were Michael Jordan and Len Bias,” Mike Krzyzewski, Duke University head basketball coach, told The Washington Post.

### Derek Boogaard

Derek Boogaard was a professional ice hockey player who played six seasons in the NHL. He was considered one of the most intimidating players in the league given his tendency to engage in physical altercations during games.

In 2011, Boogaard died after mixing alcohol with [oxycodone](https://www.drugrehab.com/addiction/prescription-drugs/oxycodone/). Before his death, he battled substance abuse. The New York Times reported he received large amounts of prescription drugs from team doctors before and after his entry into the league’s substance abuse program.

### Don Rogers

Don Rogers was an All-American football player at the University of California, Los Angeles before spending two seasons in the NFL. In 1984, he was the American Football Conference defensive rookie of the year.

In 1986, he died of cardiac arrest caused by cocaine overdose. The amount of cocaine in his system was enough to kill an elephant, per the Los Angeles Times. He passed hours before his bachelor party and a day before his wedding.

“I don’t know why people use drugs, but, of course, the pressure [on Don] might have had something to do with it,” his fiancee, Leslie Nelson, told the Los Angeles Times.

### Darrell Porter

Darrell Porter, a 17-year MLB player, struggled with substance abuse for much of his career. In his book, “Snap Me Perfect! The Darrell Porter Story,” he claimed to have formed his drug addiction upon entering professional baseball.

Porter’s heavy cocaine use affected his behavior and memory. He once fought a man and minutes later could not recall why. Another time, he carried a shotgun around his house, paranoid the baseball commissioner would break into his home.

The former World Series MVP entered a [drug and alcohol treatment center](https://www.drugrehab.com/treatment-centers/) in 1980 and reportedly remained sober for the next 22 years. In 2002, he died of cocaine overdose.

### Cris Carter | NFL

Cris Carter dominated the gridiron during his 16-year NFL career, racking up more than 1,100 receptions, nearly 14,000 yards and 130 touchdowns. The former wide receiver was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2013.

However, his career started off rocky. He battled [marijuana addiction](https://www.drugrehab.com/addiction/drugs/marijuana/) as well as addictions to crack cocaine, alcohol and ecstasy his first three seasons and was released by the Philadelphia Eagles in 1990. After multiple stints at rehab facilities, Carter got his life and career back on track.

In a 2013 interview with the New York Post, Carter said of his crack addiction: “It takes you to dark places … it takes you to dangerous places. You’re risking your life. I finally decided I wasn’t going to be controlled by any substance any longer, so I stopped.”

### Darryl Strawberry | MLB

Darryl Strawberry was an eight-time MLB All-Star and four-time World Series champion. However, his baseball career was plagued by cocaine and alcohol abuse. He was suspended by the league three times for failing drug tests.

He checked in and out of rehab centers throughout the 1990s and early 2000s. After spending 18 months in prison for probation violations in 2002, Strawberry recovered successfully. He discovered his faith and started the Darryl Strawberry Foundation, which assists those with autism.

He once summed up his career by saying, “I never had a problem hitting. I had a problem living.”

### Chris Herren | NBA

Chris Herren played professional basketball from 1999 to 2006. During much of his career, he grappled with addictions to OxyContin, Vicodin and Percocet.

In 2008, Herren was using heroin when he crashed his vehicle into a pole. He was pronounced dead for 30 seconds. He recalls the day as the best of his life because it began his journey toward [recovery](https://www.drugrehab.com/recovery/).

Since achieving sobriety, he wrote a memoir and started The Herren Project, a nonprofit devoted to helping those affected by addiction. In 2012, the organization launched Project Purple, an anti-substance abuse campaign. He continues to tour the U.S. sharing his struggles with substance abuse at speaking engagements.

## Performance-Enhancing Drugs

Some athletes want to win at any cost. In doing so, many have turned to performance-enhancing drugs. It is a process also known as doping.

Common PEDs include:

*   [Anabolic steroids](https://www.drugrehab.com/guides/steroids/)
*   Androstenedione
*   Human growth hormone (HGH)
*   Erythropoietin

*   Diuretics
*   Creatine
*   Stimulants

Anabolic steroids are among the most popular PEDs. There are many physical and psychological side effects of their use, including irritability, insomnia, heart attack, impaired judgement and high-risk behavior.

In 2007, professional wrestler Chris Benoit killed his wife and 7-year-old son before committing suicide. A toxicology report indicated elevated levels of testosterone in his system. Steroids were found in his home, leaving officials speculating whether drugs factored into the tragedy.

### History of Performance-Enhancing Drugs in Professional Sports

Doping predates modern sports. In the third century B.C., Greek Olympic athletes used brandy and wine creations and ate hallucinogenic mushrooms and sesame seeds to enhance performance. They consumed certain plants to improve their speed and relieve pain.

However, doping was considered unethical and cheaters were often sold into slavery.

In the 1930s, cyclists were permitted to use PEDs in the Tour de France.

The Soviet Olympic team experimented with testosterone drugs in the 1950s to improve strength. Shortly after, the East German government began giving PEDs to young athletes. This led to improved performance, especially among female athletes but caused severe medical abnormalities and early deaths.

In 1966, the first drug testing of athletes occurred at the European Championships. Two years later, the International Olympic Committee began drug testing at the Summer and Winter Olympics. In the 1970s, many Olympians were disqualified from competition for anabolic steroid use.

Since then, many leagues around the world have banned performance-enhancing drugs. However, the drugs continue to evolve, and athletes are finding new ways to circumvent drug testing.

### Substance Abuse Policies

Professional sports leagues have taken substance abuse seriously in recent years. The highest leagues of the four most popular spectator sports in America — basketball, football, baseball and ice hockey — conduct drug screenings.

Drug tests may occur multiple times throughout a year.
